advisories.description: By sending a deeply nested ASN1 structure to a Apache Kerby client or service, it's possible to trigger a StackOverFlow Exception which can lead to denial of service issues. Users are recommended to upgrade to version 2.1.2, which fixes this issue.

advisories.name: Apache Qpid Proton-J: Unbounded type nesting can lead to pre-authentication stackoverflow
advisories.description:
A pre-authentication attacker could leverage type nesting to cause a StackOverflowError potentially leading to denial of service.

This issue affects Apache Qpid Proton-J: through 0.34.1.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.35.0, which fixes the issue.

advisories.name: Apache Shiro's "remember me" cookie age is not verified on the server.
advisories.description:
"Remember me" cookie age is not verified on the server. This potentially allows an attacker to intercept a valid cookie and reuse it indefinitely, even after the configured expiration time has passed.
This issue affects all Apache Shiro versions from 1.2.4 through 2.x, and 3.0.0-alpha-1, only when RememberMe functionality is enabled.


Upgrade to version 3.0.0 or later, which fixes the issue.

advisories.name: Apache Shiro shiro-guice module vulnerable to authentication bypass
advisories.description:
When using Apache Shiro with the shiro-guice module in a web servlet context, a specially crafted HTTP request may cause an authentication bypass.
This vulnerability is similar to  https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2020-1957, except that it affects the `shiro-guice` module instead of the `shiro-spring` module.

This issue affects all Apache Shiro versions through 2.x, and 3.0.0-alpha-1 only when using `shiro-guice` module in a web servlet context.

Upgrade to version 3.0.0 or later, which fixes the issue.

advisories.name: Keycloak has authentication bypass via jwt algorithm confusion
advisories.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak. This JWT algorithm confusion vulnerability in the JWT Authorization Grant flow allows an attacker with valid client credentials to bypass signature verification. By forging an assertion, the attacker can create unauthorized access tokens. This enables the attacker to impersonate any federated user linked to the affected Identity Provider, leading to unauthorized access and potential privilege escalation.

advisories.name: Quick-Media Batik Codec FIX Package has Vulnerability in PNG Codec
advisories.description:
Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature vulnerability in liuyueyi quick-media (plugins/svg-plugin/batik-codec-fix/src/main/java/org/apache/batik/ext/awt/image/codec/util modules). This vulnerability is associated with program files SeekableOutputStream.Java.

This issue affects all versions of quick-media. A patch is available: [3970e96](https://github.com/liuyueyi/quick-media/pull/123/commits/3970e967f6661328a5544fd0b977dac1a35e380b)

advisories.name: OGNL stricter-invocation block list bypass via java.lang.reflect reflection proxies
advisories.description:
### Summary

OGNL's optional *stricter invocation* mode maintains a block list that prevents expressions from directly calling methods on dangerous classes such as `Runtime`, `ProcessBuilder`, and `ClassLoader`. The block list filters on the **declaring class of the method OGNL invokes**. Because `java.lang.reflect.Method` (and `Constructor`/`Field`) are not on the list, an expression can use reflection as a proxy — `someMethod.invoke(target, args)` — to reach a blocked method. The real call (e.g. `ProcessBuilder.start()`) then executes inside the JDK reflection machinery and never passes back through OGNL's `invokeMethod`, so the block list never sees it.

### Proof of concept

Under the default OGNL context (public-only access, stricter invocation enabled), the following expression creates a file even though a direct `new ProcessBuilder(...).start()` is blocked:

```
(#pb=new java.lang.ProcessBuilder({"/usr/bin/touch","rce-proof.txt"}),
 #methods=@java.lang.ProcessBuilder@class.getMethods(),
 #names=#methods.{ #this.getName() },
 #startIdx=#names.indexOf("start"),
 #methods[#startIdx].invoke(#pb, null))
```

### Impact and scope — please read carefully

**This is hardening of a defense-in-depth secondary layer, not a break of OGNL's primary security boundary.**

In OGNL the stricter-invocation block list is a *secondary* mitigation. The **primary** access-control gate is the `MemberAccess` implementation supplied by the integrating framework or application, which OGNL consults on every constructor and method call. Frameworks that evaluate untrusted expressions are expected to install a restrictive `MemberAccess` — for example, Apache Struts' `SecurityMemberAccess`, which excludes dangerous classes and the `java.lang.reflect` package. Against such a `MemberAccess` this PoC is blocked at the very first step (the `new ProcessBuilder(...)` constructor), before reflection is ever reachable.

The default context that ships with OGNL intentionally allows all public members and is **not** designed to sandbox untrusted input. An application that evaluates attacker-controlled expressions with that permissive default already has many paths to code execution, and this technique is not required to achieve it.

**You are affected only if all of the following hold:** (1) your application evaluates untrusted/attacker-controlled OGNL expressions, (2) it uses OGNL's default permissive `MemberAccess` (or an equivalently permissive one that allows `java.lang.reflect`), and (3) it relies on the stricter-invocation block list as its sandbox. **Properly configured consumers — including Apache Struts with its `SecurityMemberAccess` — are not affected.** The actual protection for untrusted-expression scenarios remains a correctly configured `MemberAccess`; the block list should not be treated as a sandbox.

### Fix

`java.lang.reflect.Method`, `java.lang.reflect.Constructor`, and `java.lang.reflect.Field` are added to the stricter-invocation block list, so reflection objects can no longer be used as invocation proxies in stricter mode. The `java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle` path was verified not to be exploitable (its signature-polymorphic `invoke`/`invokeExact` fail through OGNL's reflection-based invocation), so no additional classes are required.

### Credit

Reported responsibly through Tidelift by 毛锐 (youyi.mr@alibaba-inc.com).

advisories.name: MariaDB Connector/J: Rogue server can drive large heap allocations from server-declared lengths in OK packets
advisories.description:
## Summary

MariaDB Connector/J sized heap allocations from lengths declared by the server
in OK packets before checking that those lengths fit in the packet. A rogue or
MitM server can make the client allocate megabytes from a packet of a few bytes.

## Details

When `CLIENT_SESSION_TRACK` is negotiated (the default), an OK packet carries an
info field followed by session-state blocks, each tracked variable being sent as a
length-encoded name and value. `OkPacket.parse()` and `parseWithInfo()` allocated
`new byte[len]` for the info field, the variable name and the value with the
server-declared `len`, then copied the packet data into it. The copy failed with an
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when the packet was shorter, but only after the
allocation had taken place.

A server-declared length of 8 MiB in an 18-byte packet was enough to trigger an
8 MiB allocation; the integer-range validation of length-encoded values does not
help, since such lengths are valid positive integers.

The fix validates every server-declared length against the remaining packet bytes
before any allocation (`ReadableByteBuf.checkLength()` and a bounded
`readBytes(int)`), and stops reading the session state at the first inconsistent
entry.

## Impact

Availability only: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can drive
attacker-controlled heap allocations on every OK packet, creating GC pressure up to
`OutOfMemoryError` in the client application. Exploitation requires control of the
server side of the connection; no authentication bypass, confidentiality or
integrity impact.

## Credit

Reported by fg0x0

advisories.name: MariaDB Connector/J: Length-encoded integers larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE were truncated before being used as lengths
advisories.description:
## Summary

MariaDB Connector/J narrowed 8-byte length-encoded integers received from the
server to `int` without validation. A rogue or MitM server can send a value above
`Integer.MAX_VALUE` whose truncation becomes a negative or arbitrary length.

## Details

The protocol encodes lengths as length-encoded integers, whose 8-byte form the
decoder (`readLength()` and `readIntLengthEncodedNotNull()`) returned as
`(int) readLong()`. A value above `Integer.MAX_VALUE` therefore wrapped to a
negative or unrelated `int`, used afterwards as a length to size allocations or
reads, which ended in `NegativeArraySizeException`, out-of-bounds exceptions or
oversized allocations.

The fix rejects any length-encoded value that does not fit a non-negative `int`
with an explicit error.

## Impact

Availability only: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can crash the
client's connection handling with unchecked exceptions or drive oversized
allocations. Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection;
no authentication bypass, confidentiality or integrity impact.

## Credit

Reported by fg0x0

advisories.name: MariaDB Connector/J: XA recover() trusted server-supplied gtrid and bqual lengths
advisories.description:
## Summary

`XAResource.recover()` in MariaDB Connector/J trusted the `gtrid_length` and
`bqual_length` columns returned by `XA RECOVER` to allocate and split each Xid.

## Details

`MariaDbPoolConnection` and `MariaDbPoolPinnedConnection` built each `Xid` of
the recovery list by allocating `new byte[gtrid_length]` and
`new byte[bqual_length]` and copying from the `data` column, without validating
the lengths against the XA specification bounds (`Xid.MAXGTRIDSIZE`,
`Xid.MAXBQUALSIZE`) or the actual payload. Negative or oversized lengths, or
lengths that do not fit the data, ended in large allocations or unchecked
exceptions (`NegativeArraySizeException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`)
during recovery.

The fix validates the lengths before any allocation or copy and reports an
invalid row as an `XAException` (`XAER_RMFAIL`).

## Impact

Availability only, and limited to applications running XA recovery: a malicious
or compromised server, or a MitM, can crash the recovery or drive large
allocations. Exploitation requires control of the server side of the connection.

## Credit

Reported by fg0x0

advisories.name: MariaDB Connector/J: LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE file check could be satisfied by text inside quoted identifiers, letting a malicious server read client files
advisories.description:
## Summary

MariaDB Connector/J checked a server's LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE file request by
searching the text of the command it had sent for
`LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '<file>'`. The search also matched inside quoted
identifiers, string literals and comments, so text returned by the server and
re-used in a later query could satisfy it. A rogue or MitM server can read any
file the client JVM can read.

## Details

When a server answers a command with a LOCAL INFILE request (`0xFB` packet), the
connector opens the named file on the client host and streams it to the server,
after verifying that the file corresponds to a `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` of the
command it sent (`ClientMessage.validateLocalFileName()`). That verification was a
regular expression whose prefix accepted any character, so it answered "does the
text appear anywhere in the SQL", including inside a backtick-quoted identifier.

Several driver paths put identifiers returned by the server straight back into
their next query: `DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys()` and `getExportedKeys()`
re-use database and table names from `SHOW DATABASES`, `SHOW TABLES` and the
`REFERENCES` clause of `SHOW CREATE TABLE` output, and updatable result sets build
their `UPDATE` and refresh `SELECT` from the schema and table names of the column
definition packets. A server returning an identifier such as
``LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/etc/passwd'`` makes the connector send
``SHOW CREATE TABLE `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/etc/passwd'`.`accounts` ``; the
server answers it with a LOCAL INFILE request for `/etc/passwd`, the check
passes, and the file content is sent. On the `getImportedKeys()` path the
resulting error is swallowed and the application observes nothing. The same
applies to an application that interpolates identifiers obtained from the
server into its own queries.

The fix parses the command instead of searching it: string literals, quoted
identifiers and comments are skipped, statements are split on `;`, and only a
`LOAD DATA|XML [LOW_PRIORITY|CONCURRENT] LOCAL INFILE` found at the start of a
statement is considered, its file literal or bound parameter being compared
exactly to the requested file.

## Impact

Confidentiality: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can read arbitrary
files from the host running the JDBC client (application configuration,
credential files, key stores, ...) through standard `java.sql` calls such as
`DatabaseMetaData.getImportedKeys()`, `getExportedKeys()` or
`ResultSet.updateRow()`. Exploitation requires control of the server side of the
connection and `allowLocalInfile` enabled (the default). Setting
`allowLocalInfile=false` is a workaround when LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE is not
needed. No integrity or availability impact.

## Credit

Reported by buxuwa (buxu) through HackerOne

advisories.name: MariaDB Connector/J: Server could switch character_set_results away from UTF-8 without the client noticing
advisories.description:
## Summary

MariaDB Connector/J decodes every result as UTF-8 and guards
`character_set_client` against a change to another charset, but did not guard
`character_set_results`, and relied on the server's global
`session_track_system_variables` list to be told about charset changes at all.

## Details

The connector learns about session variable changes through session tracking,
and closes the connection when `character_set_client` is switched away from UTF-8,
so that its UTF-8 decoding stays correct. Two gaps remained:

- `character_set_results` was not guarded: a server could switch it to another
  charset, after which the bytes of every result were decoded as UTF-8 although
  encoded otherwise.
- the list of tracked variables came from the server's global
  `session_track_system_variables`: a server configured, or made, not to track
  the character set variables could change them silently.

The fix requests an explicit session tracking list that includes both character
set variables whatever the server's global setting, and closes the connection
when `character_set_results` is changed to a charset other than `utf8`, `utf8mb3`
or `utf8mb4`, as it already did for `character_set_client`.

## Impact

Integrity: a malicious or compromised server, or a MitM, can make the strings an
application reads differ from the bytes the server returned (inappropriate
encoding for the output context), which can defeat application-side validation
or escaping built on those values. Exploitation requires control of the server
side of the connection; no confidentiality or availability impact.

## Credit

Reported by fg0x0

advisories.name: Keycloak logs sensitive headers
advisories.description:
A flaw was found in Keycloak. When the logging format is configured to a verbose, user-supplied pattern (such as the pre-defined 'long' pattern), sensitive headers including Authorization and Cookie are disclosed to the logs in cleartext. An attacker with read access to the log files can extract these credentials (e.g., bearer tokens, session cookies) and use them to impersonate users, leading to a full account compromise.

Patches are available, see:

- https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/26.4.11
- https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/26.5.6
- https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/releases/tag/26.6.0

advisories.name: Keycloak vulnerable to cross-site scripting (xss) via case-insensitive uri validation bypass
advisories.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak. A remote attacker with administrative privileges, specifically those with `manage-client` permission or access to client registration endpoints, could bypass client Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) validation. This is achieved by registering a malicious client with a specially crafted redirect URI using a case-insensitive `javascript:` or `data:` scheme. This Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability allows for arbitrary code execution in the Keycloak origin when a victim clicks the crafted link, such as in the logout flow or the Admin Console.

advisories.name: Keycloak vulnerable to information disclosure through arbitrary filesystem path probing
advisories.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak. A realm administrator with the "manage-realm" role can exploit this vulnerability by submitting an arbitrary filesystem path as a keystore parameter when creating a key provider component. This allows the administrator to probe arbitrary filesystem paths, determining which files exist and are readable by the Keycloak process. This information disclosure could be used to identify high-value targets for follow-on attacks.

advisories.name: Keycloak allows unauthorized access to resources via uma permission ticket bypass
advisories.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in org.keycloak.authorization. An authenticated user with a granted User-Managed Access (UMA) permission ticket for one resource can exploit this by using a specific permission request prefix to bypass per-resource access control. This allows the user to gain unauthorized access to all resources of that type within the same resource server, even if they do not have a ticket for those specific resources. This vulnerability requires the resource server to be configured in PERMISSIVE policy enforcement mode and affects typed resources with ownerManagedAccess enabled, where no explicit policy protects the resource type. The primary consequence is unauthorized information disclosure or modification of resources.

advisories.name: Keycloak vulnerable to authorization bypass via incorrect uri comparison
advisories.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak Policy Enforcer. This vulnerability allows any authenticated user to bypass all authorization policies, including role, scope, and User-Managed Access (UMA) permission checks. By including the configured access-denied page path within a request URL, either as a path segment or a query parameter, an attacker can gain unauthorized access to protected resources.

advisories.name: Keycloak: Attacker can re-enable and take over disabled clients via registration access token
advisories.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak's client registration service. A remote attacker, possessing a previously issued Registration Access Token (RAT), could exploit this vulnerability to re-enable a client that an administrator had explicitly disabled. This bypasses security controls, allowing the attacker to reset the client's secret and potentially regain privileged API access. The primary impact includes unauthorized information disclosure and potential integrity compromise.

advisories.name: opentelemetry-java: Quadratic CPU consumption in W3C tracestate parsing
advisories.description:
### Summary

OpenTelemetry Java's W3C trace-context propagator permits excessive CPU consumption when extracting crafted `tracestate` headers, potentially leading to denial of service. Regex backtracking causes quadratic parsing time for headers containing long runs of spaces or tabs without a following comma.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker whose headers reach `W3CTraceContextPropagator.extract()` can cause excessive CPU usage through crafted requests. Parsing blocks the calling thread, potentially affecting other connections when extraction runs on a shared event-loop thread. Actual impact depends on ingress header-size limits, proxy configuration, and threading. Header-size limits reduce the per-request cost but do not eliminate the vulnerability.

### Patches

Upgrade `io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-api` to version **1.67.0** or later. [PR #8914](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java/pull/8914) replaces regex delimiter splitting with literal comma scanning and explicit whitespace trimming.

### Workarounds

If upgrading is not possible, reject or remove oversized `tracestate` headers before trace-context extraction. This reduces the per-request parsing cost but does not eliminate the risk from repeated requests.

advisories.name: Apache Thrift has an issue with Java TSSLTransportFactory hostname verification
advisories.description:
Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch vulnerability in Apache Thrift.

This issue affects Apache Thrift: before 0.23.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 0.23.0, which fixes the issue.

advisories.name: OpenAM Unauthenticated Session Hijacking via Information Exposure in CDCServlet
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

An Information Exposure Through Sent Data (CWE-201) issue in OpenAM's Cross-Domain Single Sign-On (CDSSO) servlet allows a logged-in user's raw OpenAM session token to be POSTed to an attacker-controlled URL. This impacts OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6. This issue was patched in version 16.1.1.

An attacker who can induce a logged-in victim to visit a crafted URL may receive the victim's session credential, which could enable session hijacking.

## Impact
OpenAM deployments through version 16.0.6 that have CDSSO enabled are potentially affected. The CDSSO component is commonly enabled in multi-domain deployments. Exploitation requires user interaction — an authenticated user must be induced to visit an attacker-crafted URL — and is further gated on a non-default configuration being absent.

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM Insecure SSO Cookie Initialization
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**
An Insecure Default Initialization of Resource (CWE-1188) issue in the OpenAM default configuration ships the `iPlanetDirectoryPro` SSO cookie with `HttpOnly=false`. Also, the `iPlanetDirectoryPro` SSO cookie is used as a CSRF token in OAuth/OIDC flows. This affects OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6 and was patched in version 16.1.1.

## Impact
A single click on an attacker link may yield full SSO session theft of any authenticated console user when chained with any other same-origin XSS in the OpenAM origin. The missing `SameSite` default also widens the CSRF surface. Also, because the consent flow reuses the SSO cookie as its CSRF token, any XSS in the OpenAM origin both steals the session and completes attacker-driven OAuth consent grants in one step.

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM Authentication Bypass via MSISDN LDAP Injection
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

An LDAP Injection (CWE-90) vulnerability in the MSISDN authentication module allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker to obtain an arbitrary OpenAM session without a password in the default trusted gateway configuration. This impacts OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6. This issue was patched in version 16.1.1.

## Impact
OpenAM deployments through version 16.0.6 that have MSISDN enabled are potentially affected. This enables a pre-authentication login bypass for any realm where an MSISDN module instance is enabled in an authentication chain and reachable through the trusted-gateway list, which allows all traffic by default. The request-supplied MSISDN value was concatenated directly into an LDAP search filter. The resulting OpenAM session is a normal authenticated session for the matched user.

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM Authenticated Privilege Escalation via Raw Token Disclosure Session RPC
advisories.description:
## Summary

Description

An insufficient authorization (CWE-285) and information exposure (CWE-200) issue in OpenAM's session management endpoint allows a low-privileged authenticated user to retrieve active session credentials belonging to other users, including those with higher privileges. This affects OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6 and was patched in version 16.1.1.

This may be related to CVE-2021-4201, a similar issue patched in ForgeRock Access Management, a separate product sharing a common codebase ancestry.

## Impact

OpenAM Community Edition deployments through version 16.0.6 using stateful session storage and exposing the session management endpoint are potentially affected. The endpoint does not enforce ownership or privilege checks when querying session information, meaning an authenticated user may retrieve active session credentials for arbitrary users. Successful exploitation requires a valid low-privilege session and knowledge of a target user's identity identifier, which may be obtainable through normal platform functionality.

If credentials belonging to a highly privileged account are obtained, this could enable further administrative actions within the platform

## Patch

This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM has Unsafe Java Deserialization via SNS
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

A Deserialization of Untrusted Data (CWE-502) issue exists in OpenAM's Push Notification SNS callback resource. The REST route that handles SNS push messages is mounted with anonymous access and, when a supplied message identifier has expired from the in-memory dispatcher, falls back to a CTS-stored predicate blob whose top-level keys are treated as Java class names and passed to Class.forName(...) before attacker-controlled JSON is deserialized via Jackson. This impacts OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6. This issue was patched in version 16.1.1.

Arbitrary attacker-controlled code execution was not confirmed on tested stock classpaths for the latest release, but the flaw yields a reliable class-loading and Jackson-construction primitive whose impacts include remotely triggerable process execution, file writes, and DoS, depending on the deployment's classpath and environment.

## Impact
OpenAM Community Edition deployments through version 16.0.6 that enable the Push Notification Service with SNS callbacks are potentially affected. While the callback route itself is anonymous, the planting step requires a low-privileged user who can start Push Registration and read their own QR-code payload. After that user obtains the server-issued messageId, shared secret, and challenge, they can wait for the in-memory dispatcher entry to expire and then send anonymous SNS callbacks that overwrite the persistent CTS blob with attacker-controlled JSON. A later anonymous callback for the same messageId causes OpenAM to load an attacker-named class and construct it with attacker-controlled values.

The planted blob is processed server-side with internal CTS privileges, giving a reliable class-loading and Jackson-construction primitive that can corrupt the push-token record and trigger classpath-dependent side effects in the OpenAM JVM. Arbitrary attacker-controlled command execution was not confirmed on the tested stock classpaths; practical severity depends on enabled Push Registration flows, JDK version, bundled or co-deployed classes, and whether any reachable class-loading or construction side effects are security-relevant in the deployment.

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM Account Takeover via Unverified Password Change in OAuth2 Module
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

An Unverified Password Change (CWE-620) and Use of Weak Credentials (CWE-1391) issue in OpenAM's OAuth2 authentication module silently rewrites a local user's password to the literal string of their username on OAuth2 re-login of an existing account. The default ldapService chain then accepts the username as the password for that user, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to obtain a session via the standard authenticate endpoint with both username and password set to the username, without any IdP interaction. This affects OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6 and was patched in version 16.1.1.

## Impact
OpenAM Community Edition deployments through version 16.0.6 that use the OAuth2 authentication module with account creation enabled (the default) are potentially affected. After two OAuth logins of a given user, that user's local password becomes their username, and the account is reachable through the default ldapService chain with username as both identifier and password. For pre-existing users whose IdP profile resolves against an existing local identifier, the rewrite fires on the very first re-login.

Usernames shorter than the default minimum password length have the rewrite silently denied (so very short administrative accounts are not affected), and the same update path marks accounts active on every OAuth login, silently reactivating disabled accounts. 

Successful exploitation grants an unauthenticated attacker a session carrying the victim principal's privileges.

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM has pre-auth Reflected XSS in OAuth2 / OIDC response_mode=form_post via state parameter (FormPostResponse.ftl)
advisories.description:
### Summary

The OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect authorization endpoint does not sufficiently sanitize certain user-supplied parameters before incorporating them into the HTML response generated for the `form_post` response mode. This may allow an attacker to inject content into the rendered page in the context of the OpenAM origin.

advisories.name: OpenAM SAML2 Cluster Cookie-Hash-Redirect Path has Pre-authentication Reflected XSS via `FSUtils.postToTarget`
advisories.description:
## Summary

Certain federation endpoints do not consistently apply output encoding when rendering user-supplied parameters into HTML responses. Under a non-default configuration used in some clustered deployments, this inconsistency can result in reflected XSS in the OpenAM origin without authentication.

advisories.name: OpenAM OAuth Client Impersonation via JWKS Resolver Cache
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

An Improper Authentication (CWE-287) issue in OpenAM's OAuth2 private_key_jwt client authentication path allows any registered OAuth2 client to mint tokens in the name of any other client whose key is published via a jwks_uri, without knowing the victim's signing key. This affects OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6 and was patched in version 16.1.1.

## Impact

OpenAM Community Edition deployments through version 16.0.6 that have OAuth2 clients configured for private_key_jwt authentication with keys published via jwks_uri are potentially affected. An attacker holding any such client registration, their own, or one obtained through open dynamic client registration where enabled, can mint access tokens in any other such client's name, in any realm hosted by the OpenAM process.

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM Arbitrary OAuth Token Minting via Push Registration
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

An Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (CWE-639) exists in OpenAM's stateful OAuth2 token-read path. Under certain conditions, this may allow an attacker to forge OAuth2 bearer tokens and OIDC ID tokens with arbitrary subject, client, realm, and scope. This affects OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6.

The OAuth2 token-read path reads caller-supplied token identifiers from the shared Core Token Store (CTS) without placing them in an OAuth-only namespace and without binding the row's trusted CTS type to the expected OAuth token family, so any CTS row whose BLOB claims to be an OAuth token is accepted on the read path with no integrity check.

## Impact

OpenAM Community Edition deployments through version 16.0.6 with the OAuth2 Provider service enabled in a realm are potentially affected, but the vulnerable read path is only reachable once an attacker can place attacker-controlled JSON into the shared CTS under an identifier they know. For example, an anonymous Push Notification SNS callback handler, reachable by any low-privileged user in a Push Notification-enabled realm after a single legitimate Push registration can trigger the exploit.

In any deployment where such a primitive exists, an attacker can forge OAuth2 bearer tokens with attacker-chosen userName, clientID, realm, and scope. The compromise does not by itself create an OpenAM SSO session or grant admin-console access.

## Patch

This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM Authenticated Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via `/sessionservice`
advisories.description:
OpenAM (Open Identity Platform) is an open-source Identity and Access Management (IAM) platform derived from ForgeRock OpenAM, providing SSO, OAuth2, SAML, and OpenID Connect capabilities. It is widely deployed in enterprise environments as a central authentication gateway.

The `/sessionservice` endpoint, used for internal session management operations, does not sufficiently restrict the URLs that authenticated users may register for session event notifications. Under certain conditions, this may result in outbound server-side requests to attacker-controlled destinations, potentially exposing session-related data.

This behavior results in a **server-side request forgery (SSRF)** vulnerability, where an authenticated attacker can trigger outbound requests to arbitrary destinations.

## Credit

Discovered by **JD-Security SHENYI Team**

advisories.name: OpenAM has LDAP Injection via `_queryId` Parameter
advisories.description:
OpenAM (Open Identity Platform) is an open-source IAM platform providing SSO, OAuth2, SAML, and OpenID Connect capabilities. The CREST REST API layer exposes user query endpoints under `/json/{realm}/users`. In `IdentityResourceV1.queryCollection()`, the HTTP query parameter `_queryId` is passed to a `CrestQuery` object with `escapeQueryId` **explicitly set to `false`**, bypassing the escape protection introduced as part of the CVE-2021-29156 fix. The unescaped value flows directly to `DJLDAPv3Repo.getFilter()` where it is concatenated into an LDAP filter string without sanitization, enabling authenticated attackers to inject arbitrary LDAP metacharacters for user enumeration and blind LDAP injection.

## Affected Endpoint

| Endpoint | Auth Required | Injection Parameter |
|----------|--------------|---------------------|
| `GET /openam/json/{realm}/users?_queryId=<INJECTION>` | SSO Token | `_queryId` |
| `GET /openam/json/{realm}/groups?_queryId=<INJECTION>` | SSO Token (TBD) | `_queryId` |

## Background: CVE-2021-29156

CVE-2021-29156 was a pre-authentication LDAP injection in OpenAM's Webfinger endpoint, where user-supplied input reached `DJLDAPv3Repo.getFilter()` unescaped. The fix introduced the `escapeQueryId` flag in `CrestQuery` (defaulting to `true`) and added `Filter.escapeAssertionValue()` in the filter-building path:

## Credit

Discovered by **JD-Security SHENYI Team**

advisories.name: OpenAM: Pre-auth RCE via Java Deserialization in WebAuthn Authenticator Storage
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability (CWE-502) exists in OpenAM's WebAuthn authentication module. Under certain conditions, this may allow an attacker to achieve arbitrary code execution in the context of the application server. This affects OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6 and was patched in version 16.1.1.

This is not the default configuration. Exploitation requires that an attacker has previously been able to write attacker-controlled data to a storage attribute read by the WebAuthn module, and that the WebAuthn authentication flow is reachable.

## Impact
WebAuthn is a modern shipped module, but the vulnerable configuration requires either the default storage attribute to become attacker-writable, or the WebAuthn userAttribute to be set to an attacker-writable string attribute. That is not the default, but it is feasible in deployments because the product exposes the storage attribute as a free-form admin setting and does not warn or enforce that it must be server-managed and non-user-writable. This may exist through delegated administration, provisioning, write access to the backing LDAP/directory user record, legacy REST self-registration, or unsafe reconfiguration of `userAttribute`.

In any deployment where the attribute becomes user writable, an attacker can execute arbitrary code as the application server user. 

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: OpenAM: Unauthenticated Authentication Bypass via RADIUS Spoofing
advisories.description:
## Summary

**Description**

An Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (CWE-347) issue in OpenAM's RADIUS authentication module allows an unauthenticated network attacker to spoof an Access-Accept response and obtain an OpenAM session for any RADIUS username, without knowing the configured shared secret. This affects OpenAM Community Edition through version 16.0.6 and was patched in version 16.1.1.

The RADIUS client opens an unconnected datagram socket and treats the first UDP datagram delivered to its source port as authoritative. The receive path does not check the source IP/port, does not match the response identifier to the outstanding request, and does not verify the Response Authenticator (RFC 2865 §3); the RFC 2869 Message-Authenticator is neither sent nor required. Any non-Reject/non-Challenge packet is treated as success, so a forged Access-Accept is accepted as a valid login.

## Impact
OpenAM Community Edition deployments through version 16.0.6 where an administrator has enabled a RADIUS module instance on a login chain are potentially affected. An attacker either races the real server on-path, or off-path sprays forged Access-Accept packets at the OpenAM client port. Because the client performs no verification of the response authenticator, no MD5 chosen-prefix forgery is required, which is is materially stronger than the BlastRADIUS family (CVE-2024-3596), in which an attacker must still forge a valid authenticator.

Successful exploitation yields pre-authentication impersonation of any RADIUS-mapped user in any affected realm. The resulting session is indistinguishable from a legitimate RADIUS login and carries the named principal's privileges.

## Patch
This has been patched in OpenAM Community Edition version 16.1.1. Users are encouraged to update to the latest release.

advisories.name: snappy-java: Heap buffer overflow in Snappy.uncompress*Array typed-array methods
advisories.description:
### Impact
`Snappy.uncompressCharArray`, `uncompressShortArray`, `uncompressIntArray`, `uncompressLongArray`, `uncompressFloatArray` and `uncompressDoubleArray` sized the result array by dividing the declared uncompressed byte length by the element size, but native code wrote the full byte length. If the declared length is not a multiple of the element size, up to 7 bytes are written past the end of the Java array, corrupting the heap.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.1.10.9 ([#739](https://github.com/xerial/snappy-java/pull/739)). These methods now reject uncompressed lengths that are not a multiple of the element size with `SnappyIOException`.

### Workarounds
Check that `Snappy.uncompressedLength(input)` is a multiple of the element size before calling these methods.

advisories.name: snappy-java: JVM crash from unchecked ranges in Snappy.arrayCopy and SnappyOutputStream.rawWrite
advisories.description:
### Impact
`Snappy.arrayCopy(Object src, int offset, int byteLength, Object dest, int destOffset)` called a native `memcpy` without validating the ranges. A negative or oversized `byteLength` or offset read or wrote outside the arrays and crashed the JVM. `SnappyOutputStream.rawWrite` and `SnappyInputStream.rawRead`, and therefore the typed-array `write`/`read` methods, pass caller-supplied ranges to this method.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#741). `Snappy.arrayCopy` checks both ranges before copying. The stream `read`/`write` methods validate offsets and lengths, and reject typed-array ranges whose byte size overflows `int`.

### Workarounds
Validate offsets and lengths before calling these methods.

advisories.name: snappy-java: Unbounded memory allocation from attacker-declared uncompressed lengtha
advisories.description:
### Impact
Several decompression paths in snappy-java allocate an output buffer sized by the uncompressed length declared in the first bytes of the compressed data, before decompressing or validating it. A few bytes of crafted input can therefore force an allocation of up to 2 GB, causing `OutOfMemoryError` (denial of service), or a `NegativeArraySizeException` for declared lengths of 2^31 or more.

Affected entry points include `Snappy.uncompress(byte[])`, `Snappy.uncompressString`, the `Snappy.uncompress*Array` methods, `SnappyInputStream`, and `SnappyFramedInputStream`. The `maxChunkSize` limit added for CVE-2023-43642 bounds only the compressed chunk length, so it does not prevent this.

### Patches
Fixed in 1.1.10.9 (#739). `Snappy.uncompressedLength()` now rejects negative declared lengths, and lengths larger than any valid Snappy stream of the given size can produce. The densest Snappy element expands 3 bytes to 64, so the limit is 64/3 of the compressed size. Allocations are therefore proportional to the input actually received.

### Workarounds
Before decompressing untrusted data, check that `Snappy.uncompressedLength(input)` is within an application-specific limit.

advisories.name: IzPack has Path Traversal in UnpackerBase that allows writing files outside the installation directory via malicious pack entries
advisories.description:
### Summary

IzPack's `UnpackerBase.unpack()` resolves pack-file target paths without any
canonical-path or directory-containment check. An attacker who distributes a
trojanized installer JAR (the format is unsigned) can include pack entries whose
`targetPath` contains `../` sequences. When a victim runs the installer the
file is written to an attacker-chosen location on disk under the victim's
privileges — including startup folders, PATH directories, or system locations.

### Details

**Vulnerable method:** `com.izforge.izpack.installer.unpacker.UnpackerBase.unpack()`
**Source file:** `izpack-installer/src/main/java/com/izforge/izpack/installer/unpacker/UnpackerBase.java`
**Vulnerable lines (5.2.4):** ~618–627

The relevant code path is:

```java
String targetPath = packFile.getTargetPath();             // attacker-controlled
String path       = IoHelper.translatePath(targetPath, variables); // separator swap ONLY
File   target     = new File(path);                       // no canonical check
// ... mkdirs() then file is written to `target`
```

`IoHelper.translatePath()` (source: `izpack-util/.../IoHelper.java`) performs
**only** file-separator character conversion (`'/'` ↔ `File.separatorChar`) and
contains no security validation whatsoever. There is no call to
`getCanonicalPath()`, no `startsWith(installDir)` containment check, and no
normalisation of `..` segments.

Because IzPack installer JARs carry **no digital signature**, an attacker can
repack any legitimate installer with malicious `PackFile` entries. The file
format is a standard ZIP with serialised resources — no integrity protection.

**Confirmed unpatched in HEAD (fetched from GitHub, 2025):**
```
git show HEAD:izpack-installer/src/main/java/com/izforge/izpack/installer/unpacker/UnpackerBase.java \
  | grep -n 'getCanonicalPath\|startsWith.*install\|traversal'
# (no output — fix not present)
```

### PoC

```bash
# 1. Clone IzPack source and view the vulnerable code directly
git clone --depth=1 --branch izpack-5.2.4 https://github.com/izpack/izpack.git
sed -n '615,650p' izpack/izpack-installer/src/main/java/com/izforge/izpack/installer/unpacker/UnpackerBase.java

# 2. Compile and run the following Java reproducer (no IzPack classpath needed):
```

```java
// TestPathTraversal.java
import java.io.*;

public class TestPathTraversal {
    // Exact replication of IoHelper.translatePath() — separator swap, no security
    static String translatePath(String destination) {
        return destination.replace('/', File.separatorChar);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String installDir   = "/tmp/izpack_install";
        String maliciousPath = installDir + "/../../../tmp/ESCAPED_FILE";

        // This is what UnpackerBase does:
        String path   = translatePath(maliciousPath);
        File   target = new File(path);           // resolves traversal
        target.getParentFile().mkdirs();
        try (FileWriter fw = new FileWriter(target)) {
            fw.write("Written outside install dir via IzPack path traversal\n");
        }
        System.out.println("File written to: " + target.getCanonicalPath());
        System.out.println("Inside installDir: " +
            target.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(new File(installDir).getCanonicalPath()));
    }
}
```

```bash
javac TestPathTraversal.java && java TestPathTraversal
# Output: File written to: /tmp/ESCAPED_FILE
#         Inside installDir: false
```

### Impact

Any user who runs an IzPack-generated installer is affected. The attacker only
needs to distribute a repackaged installer — a common social-engineering vector.
On Windows (the primary IzPack platform) the victim typically runs the installer
as a local administrator, so the attacker can write to `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup`,
`%SystemRoot%\System32`, or any other location reachable by the victim user.
On Linux/macOS the same applies for user-writable locations.

No authentication, no special privileges and no interaction beyond running the
installer are required on the victim side.

### Credits
This issue was identified by Michał Majchrowicz, Marcin Wyczechowski, and Paweł Zdunek, members of the AFINE Team.

advisories.name: Apache Tomcat - HTTP/2 no-authority bypass of strict SNI validation
advisories.description:
Improper Input Validation vulnerability in Apache Tomcat due to incomplete fix for CVE-2026-32990.

This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.20 through 11.0.24, from 10.1.53 through 10.1.57, from 9.0.115 through 9.0.120.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.25, 10.1.59 or 9.0.121, which fix the issue.

advisories.name: Google Guava: CompactHashMap/CompactHashSet/MapMakerInternalMap deserialization triggers uncontrolled memory allocation
Apache CXF has Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference
advisories.description: Apache CXF's EndpointReferenceUtils and W3CMultiSchemaFactory classes construct a SAXParserFactory without the necessary JAXP hardening configurations, enabling out-of-band (OOB) external entity resolution. Users are recommended to upgrade to versions 4.2.2 or 4.1.7 or 3.6.12, which fix this issue.

advisories.name: Apache Log4j 1 to Log4j 2 bridge: silent log event loss in Log4j1XmlLayout due to unescaped XML 1.0 forbidden characters
advisories.description:
The `Log4j1XmlLayout` from the Apache Log4j 1-to-Log4j 2 bridge fails to escape characters forbidden by the XML 1.0 standard, producing malformed XML output. Conforming XML parsers are required to reject documents containing such characters with a fatal error, which may cause downstream log processing systems to drop or fail to index affected records.

Two groups of users are affected:

* Those using `Log4j1XmlLayout` directly in a Log4j Core 2 configuration file.
* Those using the Log4j 1 configuration compatibility layer with `org.apache.log4j.xml.XMLLayout` specified as the layout class.

Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Log4j 1-to-Log4j 2 bridge version `2.25.4`, which corrects this issue.

> [!NOTE]
> The Apache Log4j 1-to-Log4j 2 bridge is deprecated and will not be present in Log4j 3. Users are encouraged to consult the
> [Log4j 1 to Log4j 2 migration guide](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/migrate-from-log4j1.html), and specifically the section on eliminating reliance on the bridge.

advisories.name: Keycloak: Unauthorized access via improper validation of encrypted SAML assertions
advisories.description: Keycloak's SAML broker endpoint does not properly validate encrypted assertions when the overall SAML response is not signed. An attacker with a valid signed SAML assertion can exploit this by crafting a malicious SAML response, injecting an encrypted assertion for an arbitrary principal, leading to unauthorized access and potential information disclosure.

advisories.name: Apache Tomcat util accepted misconfigured CRLs
advisories.description:
Detection of Error Condition Without Action vulnerability in Apache Tomcat when configuring Certificate Revocation List (CRLs) for a FFM based connector. If an FFM connector was configured with invalid CRLs, the invalid CRLs were ignored meaning invalid certificates could be accepted.

This issue affects Apache Tomcat: from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.22, from 10.1.0-M7 through 10.1.55, from 9.0.83 through 9.0.118.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.23, 10.1.56 or 9.0.119, which fixes the issue.

advisories.name: Keycloak's identity-first login flow exposes user information
advisories.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. A remote attacker can exploit differential error messages during the identity-first login flow when Organizations are enabled. This vulnerability allows an attacker to determine the existence of users, leading to information disclosure through user enumeration.

advisories.name: Keycloak has an improper input validation vulnerability
advisories.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. This improper input validation vulnerability occurs because Keycloak accepts RFC-compliant matrix parameters in URL path segments, while common reverse proxy configurations may ignore or mishandle them. A remote attacker can craft requests to mask path segments, potentially bypassing proxy-level path filtering. This could expose administrative or sensitive endpoints that operators believe are not externally reachable.

advisories.name: Keycloak: Arbitrary code execution via Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in organization selection login page
advisories.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak, specifically in the organization selection login page. A remote attacker with `manage-realm` or `manage-organizations` administrative privileges can exploit a Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability. This flaw occurs because the `organization.alias` is placed into an inline JavaScript `onclick` handler, allowing a crafted JavaScript payload to execute in a user's browser when they view the login page. Successful exploitation enables arbitrary JavaScript execution, potentially leading to session theft, unauthorized account actions, or further attacks against users of the affected realm.

advisories.name: Keycloak has Improper Access Control that allows attackers with valid credentials to bypass the allowRemoteResourceManagement=false
advisories.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. An improper Access Control vulnerability in Keycloak’s User-Managed Access (UMA) resource_set endpoint allows attackers with valid credentials to bypass the allowRemoteResourceManagement=false restriction. This occurs due to incomplete enforcement of access control checks on PUT operations to the resource_set endpoint. This issue enables unauthorized modification of protected resources, impacting data integrity.

advisories.name: A2A Java SDK: Push notification credentials logged in cleartext on protobuf parse failure
advisories.description:
### *Impact.** Push notification bearer tokens and authentication credentials submitted by clients are written to server log files in cleartext. Any operator, log aggregation system, or attacker with log access can read these secrets and use them to authenticate to the client's push notification endpoints, potentially sending forged task status updates.

**Where.** `transport/rest/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/transport/rest/handler/RestHandler.java:676` in `parseRequestBody`

**What.** The `parseRequestBody` method logs the entire JSON request body at `SEVERE` level when `JsonFormat.parser().merge()` throws `InvalidProtocolBufferException`. This method is called from `createTaskPushNotificationConfiguration` (line 377), where the body contains client-supplied push notification bearer tokens (field `token`) and authentication credentials (field `authentication.credentials`). These secrets are written to server log files in full.

**Exploit scenario.** A client creates a push notification configuration by POSTing to `/v1/tenants/{tenant}/tasks/{taskId}/pushNotificationConfigs` with a body containing `{"url": "https://client.example.com/webhook", "token": "secret-bearer-token", "authentication": {"scheme": "Bearer", "credentials": "oauth-access-token"}, "extraField": "value"}`. The extra field causes `JsonFormat.parser().merge()` to throw `InvalidProtocolBufferException`. The entire body including `secret-bearer-token` and `oauth-access-token` is logged at SEVERE level. An attacker with log access retrieves the cleartext credentials.

**Preconditions.**
- Attacker must have access to server log files (centralized logging, log aggregation, shared infrastructure, or insider access)
- Push notification capability must be enabled
- A request body must fail protobuf deserialization while being valid JSON (unknown fields with strict parsing, schema mismatches)

**Fix.** Do not log the raw request body. Log only a sanitized summary — body length and content type, not content. Replace the log call with something like: `log.log(Level.SEVERE, "Error parsing JSON request body (length={0})", body != null ? body.length() : 0)`.

**Verification.** 3/3 lens verifiers confirmed.

advisories.name: A2A Java SDK: Android synchronous POST forwards credentials across authorities after incomplete redirect fix
advisories.description:
The GHSA-9rhm fix added this safe setting in
AndroidA2AHttpClient.createConnection():

    connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(false);

The synchronous POST builder later overwrites it:

    private boolean followRedirects = true;

    public A2AHttpResponse post() throws IOException {
        HttpURLConnection connection = createConnection("POST", false);
        connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(followRedirects);
        // ...
    }

The second assignment wins. JSONRPCTransport and RestTransport both
add interceptor-produced headers and call synchronous post() without
setting followRedirects(false).

On Android's repackaged OkHttp implementation, a cross-authority
redirect strips Authorization but retains nonstandard request headers.
AuthInterceptor permits four nonstandard authentication header names:

    X-API-Key
    API-Key
    X-Auth-Token
    X-Authentication

I confirmed that the exact v1.3.1.Final Maven artifact forwards
complete synthetic values under all four names to a second loopback
authority. I also reproduced the supported AuthInterceptor to Android
POST path. Explicitly calling followRedirects(false) returns the
original 302 and produces no request to the collector.

All test traffic stayed on two ephemeral 127.0.0.1 listeners. All
credentials were synthetic FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-* values.

Reproduction

I have attached AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest.java. Copy it to:

    extras/http-client-android/src/test/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/http/android/

Run:

    mvn -pl extras/http-client-android -am \
      -Dtest=AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest \
      -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false test

On unpatched current main, the default test fails with:

    Android synchronous POST must retain the documented no-redirect default
    expected: <302> but was: <200>

The explicit followRedirects(true) control still passes.

The separate exact-artifact fixture passed three consecutive runs. Its
relevant output was:

    default status=200 x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-DIRECT
authorization=null method=GET
    control-followRedirects-false status=302 collectorHits=0
    interceptor-chain status=200
x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-INTERCEPTOR collectorHits=1
    header-matrix name=X-API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-API-Key
    header-matrix name=API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-API-Key
    header-matrix name=X-Auth-Token forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Auth-Token
    header-matrix name=X-Authentication
forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Authentication

Impact and limitations

The demonstrated impact is disclosure of a complete API key or
authentication token to a different authority. I am not claiming
subsequent use of the credential, integrity impact, availability
impact, code execution, or host compromise.

A fully malicious origin already receives the credential on the first
request. The additional boundary matters most when redirect or
front-door behavior is compromised separately from the component that
handles request credentials, or when different parts of the origin
operate in different trust domains.

The 7.5 score applies to an autonomous client where no human action is
needed after the remote endpoint returns the redirect. If the Android
workflow requires a person to select or invoke the remote agent, UI:R
gives a 6.5 score. I have kept both vectors because that deployment
detail affects severity but not the underlying behavior. These are
suggested scores, consistent with the policy's statement that actual
CVSS depends on the specific deployment context. The same policy
labels the parent credential-redirect property as moderate.

Scope and prior art

This path appears to fall directly under the project's current security model:

1. extras/http-client-android and the client transports are listed as in scope.
2. Remote AgentCard and response data are treated as attacker-relevant inputs.
3. A malicious or compromised remote agent is part of the client-side
adversary model.
4. Section 8 says automatic redirects are disabled in all JDK, Vert.x,
and Android implementations to prevent credential leakage.
5. Section 13 defines a violation of a Section 8 property through the
covered input and adversary as VALID.
6. Section 13a lists missed call sites and under-strength mitigations
as new findings after an incomplete fix.
7. Section 14 records the original issue as fixed by disabling
redirects across all HTTP client implementations. The Android
synchronous path directly contradicts that recorded repair state.

This report does not claim that an AgentCard SecurityScheme
declaration enforces authentication. The application has already
configured the credential, and the shipped AuthInterceptor places it
in an allowed header. The failure is the Android client's default
redirect behavior after that point. It does not depend on a custom
SPI, an insecure configuration flag, a test-only component,
server-side authentication, or any of the recurring non-findings
listed in Section 11a.

GHSA-9rhm is t

advisories.name: A2A Java SDK has Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in push-notification delivery
advisories.description:
---

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Affected package:** `org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common` (push-notification delivery)
- **Affected versions:** `<= 1.2.0.Final` (and `1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT` on `main` prior to the fix)
- **Patched version:** _(the release that carries the fix)_
- **CWE:** CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery)
- **Severity:** High
- **CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:L/A:N` (5.8, Moderate)

---

## Summary

An **unauthenticated** attacker can coerce the a2a-java server into issuing HTTP requests to
arbitrary internal and cloud-metadata endpoints from the server's own network position — a
Server-Side Request Forgery reachable in the default deployment with no credentials, no user
interaction, and a single request. The behaviour is the shipped default, not a misconfiguration.

## Details

`BasePushNotificationSender` (in `server-common`) POSTs task data to the URL stored on a task's
`TaskPushNotificationConfig` with no validation of the destination: no block on loopback, RFC1918,
link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, including the `169.254.169.254` metadata address), unique-local,
unspecified, or multicast ranges; no scheme restriction; and no bound on redirects.
`InMemoryPushNotificationConfigStore.setInfo` stores the URL verbatim and
`onCreateTaskPushNotificationConfig` does not check it either.

Both shipped HTTP clients follow redirects (`JdkA2AHttpClient` → `followRedirects(NORMAL)`,
`VertxA2AHttpClient` → `setFollowRedirects(true)`), so a creation-time URL allowlist is bypassable:
an attacker webhook answers `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/...` and the client follows it. A
hostname check is likewise defeated by DNS rebinding. A correct guard must validate the *resolved*
IP of every hop at connection time, not the URL string.

## Exploitation

Demonstrated end-to-end against a running server (default wiring, unauthenticated caller):

- **Arbitrary internal reachability.** The attacker picks the destination and the server issues
  the request from inside the trust boundary. Delivery to loopback and to a real RFC1918 LAN
  address was exercised at runtime; because the code applies no destination filtering of any kind,
  the same path reaches link-local / metadata (`169.254.169.254`) and other internal ranges
  wherever network routing permits.
- **Allowlist + method bypass via redirect.** A `302` from the attacker's webhook reaches
  destinations a creation-time allowlist would block, and a `302` on a `POST` is followed as a
  `GET` — so GET-only endpoints such as the IMDS credentials path are reachable even though the
  sender only issues `POST`s. This is why a URL allowlist is not a sufficient fix; the guard must
  validate the resolved IP of every redirect hop.
- **Data push into internal services.** On direct (non-redirected) delivery, each request carries
  the task payload in the body, so internal services that ingest POST data receive
  attacker-influenced content (basis for `I:L`). On a redirected request the body is dropped in the
  POST→GET conversion, so the body-push and the redirect-reach are separate capabilities, not
  simultaneous on one request.

The sender discards the fetched response and exposes no caller-visible difference between a
successful and a failed delivery (both paths return without surfacing status or body), so the base
case reads back nothing — confidentiality is scored `C:N`. Read-back is limited, reach is not: the
attacker still drives fully controlled requests to metadata and internal services and writes data
into them.

## PoC

Against a running server with push notifications enabled (JSON-RPC transport), using only the real
production classes wired the default way:

1. Start a local listener standing in for an internal target (no real metadata service is touched).
2. Send one `SendMessage` that starts a long-running task, with the push config inlined and its
   `url` set to `http://<internal-target>/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. Use
   `returnImmediately: true`, header `A2A-Version: 1.0`, and role `ROLE_USER`. The URL is stored
   verbatim. (Equivalent via `CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig` on an existing task.)
3. As the task emits state/artifact updates, the sender POSTs each one to the stored URL, from the
   server's own network position:

   ```
   POST /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ HTTP/1.1
   Host: 169.254.169.254
   Content-Type: application/json

   {"artifactUpdate":{"taskId":"...","artifact":{"parts":[{"text":"Progress update 1/20"}]}, ...}}
   ```

One `SendMessage` produced multiple server-side POSTs to the attacker-chosen internal path.
Verified on `main` (commit `72d220c`, JDK 21) and unchanged on `1.2.0.Final`.

## Remediation

Validate the *resolved* IP of the target and of every redirect hop before connecting: reject
loopback / RFC1918 / link-local / metadata / unique-local / unspecified / multicast; restrict the
scheme to `http`/`https`; cap redirects; and resolve-and-pin to defeat

advisories.name: A2A Java SDK has a fail-open default task authorization
advisories.description:
Draft text for GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w. The body below drops into the GitHub advisory description
field; the metadata block maps to the form fields. Set the patched version at release; publish
when the fix ships._

---

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Affected package:** `org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common` (task store / authorization)
- **Affected versions:** `<= 1.2.0.Final` (and `1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT` on `main` prior to the fix)
- **Patched version:** _(the release that carries the fix, e.g. 1.2.1.Final)_
- **CWE:** CWE-1188 (Insecure Default Initialization), CWE-862 (Missing Authorization)
- **Severity:** High
- **CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` (7.5, High)

---

## Details

The default task store performs no authorization on task reads. `InMemoryTaskStore`'s no-arg
constructor sets `authorizationProvider = null`, and `InMemoryTaskStore.get(String taskId)` is a
bare map lookup with no authorization check regardless of provider:

```java
public InMemoryTaskStore() {
    this.authorizationProvider = null;   // default wiring
}

@Override
public @Nullable Task get(String taskId) {
    return tasks.get(taskId);            // no owner / caller check
}
```

Authorization is enforced only when the application both supplies a `TaskAuthorizationProvider`
*and* routes requests through `AuthorizationRequestHandlerDecorator` (via CDI), which checks
ownership before delegating. A server that uses the default store, or wires
`DefaultRequestHandler.builder().build()` manually, or integrates through a non-CDI stack (e.g.
Spring), never reaches that check. The safe posture is therefore opt-in and the shipped default is
the unsafe one. A caller can read a task created by another caller simply by knowing or guessing
its id.

## Summary

With the SDK's default configuration, task reads are not authorized: any caller can retrieve a
task (including its status, context, message history, and artifacts) created by another caller,
by supplying the task id.

## PoC

Using only the real production classes wired the default way (no mocks):

1. Construct the default store: `InMemoryTaskStore store = new InMemoryTaskStore();` (no-arg
   constructor, so no authorization provider).
2. As one caller, save a task: `store.save(victimTask, false);` with id `victim-task-42`.
3. As a second, unrelated caller with no auth context, read it back: `store.get("victim-task-42")`.

The second caller receives the first caller's task in full, with no authorization check:

```
unauthenticated get(victim-task-42) returned task owned by nobody-checked: victim-task-42 / ctx=victim-ctx
```

Verified on `main` (commit `72d220c`, JDK 21) and reproduces unchanged on `1.2.0.Final`.

## Impact

Task data crosses caller boundaries with no authorization. In any multi-caller deployment built on
the default wiring, one caller can enumerate and read another caller's tasks, including task status,
context id, the message history, and any artifacts the task carries, which for agent workloads is
frequently sensitive input and generated content. Because the insecure behaviour is the default
rather than a misconfiguration, it is easy to ship unintentionally, and in the default/reference
deployment the transport endpoints are served without authentication enforced, so the read is
reachable by an unauthenticated caller (`PR:N`). CVSS is scored against the default configuration
as shipped.

## Remediation

Fail closed by default: deny task reads when no authorization provider is configured, rather than
treating a missing provider as allow-all, and apply the authorization check in the store's `get`
path (not only in `list` and the CDI decorator) so it holds regardless of how the handler is
wired. If the current permissive default is retained for single-user/testing scenarios, emit a
prominent startup warning when the server comes up with no authorization provider so it cannot be
shipped by accident.

## Workarounds

Until a fixed release, configure a `TaskAuthorizationProvider` and ensure requests are routed
through the authorization decorator (CDI wiring), rather than relying on the default no-arg store
or a manually built handler.

## References

- CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1188.html
- CWE-862: Missing Authorization: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html

advisories.name: A2A Java SDK send client credentials under server-controlled HTTP header name, enabling leakage via redirect
advisories.description:
*Impact.** A malicious or compromised A2A agent can cause the client's API key credential to be forwarded to an arbitrary third-party server. The agent serves an AgentCard with an `APIKeySecurityScheme` specifying a custom header name, then responds with an HTTP redirect. The JDK HttpClient follows the redirect and forwards the custom header containing the credential, since only the standard `Authorization` header may be stripped on cross-origin redirects.

**Where.** `client/transport/spi/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/transport/spi/interceptors/auth/AuthInterceptor.java:69` in `intercept`

**What.** The `apiKeySecurityScheme.name()` field from the remote agent's AgentCard (untrusted, server-controlled data) is used directly as the HTTP header name when placing client credentials. Combined with `JdkA2AHttpClient`'s `followRedirects(NORMAL)` policy, credentials under custom header names survive cross-origin redirects (only `Authorization` is stripped on newer JDKs), allowing a malicious agent to leak client credentials to third-party servers. Additionally, `AuthInterceptor` does not check that `location==HEADER` before placing the credential as a header.

**Exploit scenario.** Client configures an API key credential for agent's security scheme `myAuth`. The malicious agent returns an AgentCard where `securitySchemes` includes `myAuth` as `APIKeySecurityScheme` with `name='X-Leaked-Cred'` and `location=HEADER`. `AuthInterceptor` places the credential in the `X-Leaked-Cred` header. The agent responds with HTTP 302 redirect to `https://evil.com/collect`. `JdkA2AHttpClient` follows the redirect, forwarding all custom headers including `X-Leaked-Cred` to `evil.com`. The attacker captures the client's credential.

**Preconditions.**
- Client application has configured API key credentials via `CredentialService` for the agent's security scheme
- The agent is malicious or compromised (controls its own AgentCard response)
- The default `JdkA2AHttpClient` is used (with `followRedirects=NORMAL`)
- The JDK version does not strip custom headers on cross-origin redirects (all current versions)

**Fix.** Validate the `APIKeySecurityScheme.name()` field against a whitelist of safe header names. Check that `apiKeySecurityScheme.location()` equals `Location.HEADER` before placing the credential as a header. Consider using `followRedirects(NEVER)` and implementing manual redirect handling that strips all authentication headers on cross-origin redirects.

**Verification.** 2/3 lens verifiers confirmed.

advisories.name: jackson-databind: @JsonView bypassed for @JsonUnwrapped container properties on deserialization
advisories.description:
## Summary
`UnwrappedPropertyHandler.processUnwrapped()` replays the buffered JSON for a `@JsonUnwrapped` property by iterating its properties and calling `prop.deserializeAndSet()` with **no `prop.visibleInView(ctxt.getActiveView())` guard** — the exact guard `processUnwrappedCreatorProperties()` received in the #5971 / GHSA-rcqc-6cw3-h962 fix, and the guard `BeanDeserializer.deserializeWithUnwrapped` applies to directly-matched properties. As a result, a property annotated with both `@JsonView(PrivilegedView.class)` and `@JsonUnwrapped` is written from attacker JSON even when deserializing under a more-restrictive active view.

**Correction to the original framing (runtime-verified):** the gap is NOT a per-field inner `@JsonView` (the unwrapped sub-object's own `BeanDeserializer` gates inner fields correctly). The unchecked gate is the **view of the unwrapped CONTAINER property**.

## Intent proof (runtime, 2.x HEAD 21dd70dd and 3.x HEAD 7a5939d6)
An `@JsonView(AdminView)` property that is NOT `@JsonUnwrapped` → `null` under `PublicView` (correctly gated). The identical property WITH `@JsonUnwrapped` → fully populated (bypass). The fix the creator path already received, not applied to the regular-property method.

## Impact — write-side mass-assignment / privilege escalation
`@JsonView` is commonly used as a write-side authorization guard: a public endpoint binds the body under `readerWithView(PublicView.class)` and groups privileged state in a nested object whose container property is `@JsonView(AdminView)`. When that property is `@JsonUnwrapped`, an untrusted caller mass-assigns it. PoC: a self-service registration where `AccountFlags{role,approved,creditBalance}` is `@JsonView(AdminView) @JsonUnwrapped`; attacker JSON `{role:ADMIN,approved:true,creditBalance:1000000}` under `PublicView` binds all three → approved admin with arbitrary balance. The failing gate is a WRITE gate, hence integrity-high (`C:N/I:H/A:N`); no worse than the C:L/I:L parent and arguably higher as `@JsonView`-as-write-guard is the exact use case #5971/#5969 defended.

## Affected
- `com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind` 2.x: confirmed bypass at 21dd70dd (== released 2.21.4 / 2.22.0 line; includes the #5973 backport). `DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION` default=true.
- `tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind` 3.x: confirmed bypass at HEAD 7a5939d6 (latest 3.x). `DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION` default=false → the stock-config repro is the common shape where privileged inner fields are individually `@JsonView(PublicView)` and the developer relies on the container `@JsonView(AdminView)`; the 3.x PoC mass-assigns role/approved/creditBalance under PublicView. (The other simultaneous report's PoC was reportedly fixed on 3.x; this distinct container-property path is not.)

## Additive variants (runtime-confirmed both branches; all closed by the same one-line guard)
- nested `@JsonUnwrapped` (unwrapped-in-unwrapped) — recursive bypass.
- merge / `readerWithView(...).withValueToUpdate(...)` (PATCH/partial-update) — bypass; non-unwrapped merge control gates correctly.
- builder-based deserializer (`@JsonDeserialize(builder=...)`) — `BuilderBasedDeserializer` routes through the same `processUnwrapped`.
- Honest non-findings: read-side serialization correctly honors views (no leak); `@JsonAnySetter`+view and `@JsonTypeInfo`+`@JsonUnwrapped` are separate/unsupported behaviors, not this bug.

## Fix
Add `prop.visibleInView(ctxt.getActiveView())` (when `MapperFeature.DEFAULT_VIEW_INCLUSION`/active-view applies) to the `processUnwrapped()` property loop, mirroring `processUnwrappedCreatorProperties()`. One change closes the impact PoC + all three variants across `BeanDeserializer` and `BuilderBasedDeserializer`. Full runnable PoCs (2.x + 3.x) + variant harnesses available on request.
